domainTitle: Understanding how laws, standards and frameworks apply to AI

source.title: IAPP AIGP Artificial Intelligence Governance Professional Study Guide
source.author: Peter H. Gregory

tells.snippet: The organization shall establish, implement, maintain and continually improve an AI management system, including the processes needed and their interactions.
options: ISO/IEC 42001
NIST AI RMF
OECD AI Principles
EU AI Act
tells.tell: "management system" plus the "establish, implement, maintain and continually improve" formula is ISO management-standard boilerplate. It is the same sentence shape as ISO 27001 and 9001.

tells.snippet: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE are the four core functions, each broken into categories and subcategories.
options: NIST AI RMF
ISO/IEC 42001
OECD AI Principles
ISO/IEC 22989
tells.tell: Four verbs in capitals is unique to NIST. Nothing else in Domain II organises itself into GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE.
tells.citation: Ch7 §NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

tells.snippet: This document provides a vocabulary and describes concepts and terminology for AI, so that different communities can use consistent language.
options: ISO/IEC 22989
ISO/IEC 42001
ISO/IEC 42005
NIST AI RMF
tells.tell: Vocabulary and concepts only, with nothing to certify against, is 22989. If a standard tells you what words mean rather than what to do, it is the terminology standard.

tells.snippet: Guidance on the process for performing an impact assessment of an AI system on individuals and societies.
options: ISO/IEC 42005
ISO/IEC 42001
ISO/IEC 22989
ISO/IEC 23894
tells.tell: Impact assessment process = 42005. Easily confused with 42001 (the management system) and 23894 (risk management). BoK v2.1 names 22989, 42001 and 42005 as the three core ISO standards.

tells.snippet: AI actors should respect the rule of law, human rights and democratic values throughout the AI system lifecycle, including inclusive growth and sustainable development.
options: OECD AI Principles
EU AI Act
NIST AI RMF
ISO/IEC 42001
tells.tell: "AI actors" plus "inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being" is OECD language. It states values, imposes nothing, and is addressed to governments as much as firms.

tells.snippet: An evaluation programme that assesses model performance in laboratory, in controlled field testing, and in real-world use, in three layers.
options: NIST ARIA
NIST AI RMF
ISO/IEC 42005
OECD AI Principles
tells.tell: Layered evaluation moving from lab to field to real world is ARIA (Assessing Risks and Impacts of AI). The AI RMF is a framework; ARIA is a testing programme that feeds it.
tells.citation: Ch7 §NIST ARIA: Layered AI Model Evaluation

tells.snippet: Providers shall ensure that the system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure prior to its placing on the market, and shall draw up an EU declaration of conformity.
options: EU AI Act
ISO/IEC 42001
NIST AI RMF
GDPR
tells.tell: "shall" plus conformity assessment, declaration of conformity and placing on the market is EU product-safety legislation. Standards never say "shall … prior to placing on the market".

tells.snippet: A companion resource offering suggested actions, references and documentation for each subcategory, which organisations may use in whole or in part.
options: NIST AI RMF Playbook
ISO/IEC 42001
NIST ARIA
OECD Framework
tells.tell: "Suggested actions" that are voluntary and per-subcategory is the Playbook, the companion to the AI RMF. BoK II.D.2 names the Playbook alongside the framework.
tells.citation: Ch7 §NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

tells.snippet: The data subject shall have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them.
options: GDPR Article 22
EU AI Act Article 50
GDPR Article 35
EU AI Act Article 6
tells.tell: "solely on automated processing" plus "legal effects or similarly significantly affects" is Art. 22. It is a data-protection right, not an AI Act obligation — a favourite exam trap.
tells.citation: Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations in the AI Context

tells.snippet: Where processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to processing, carry out an assessment of the impact.
options: GDPR Article 35 (DPIA)
EU AI Act FRIA
ISO/IEC 42005
GDPR Article 22
tells.tell: "rights and freedoms of natural persons" plus "prior to the processing" is the GDPR DPIA. Distinguish from the AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment and from ISO 42005 guidance.
tells.citation: Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations in the AI Context

tells.snippet: Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce are hereby declared unlawful.
options: FTC Act Section 5
Title VII
Equal Credit Opportunity Act
EU AI Act
tells.tell: "unfair or deceptive acts or practices" is the literal statutory phrase of FTC Act §5 — the main US hook for overstated AI capability claims.
tells.citation: Ch5 §How Consumer Protection Laws Apply to AI

tells.snippet: A practice that is neutral on its face but falls more harshly on a protected group, and which cannot be justified by business necessity.
options: Disparate impact
Disparate treatment
Unfair practice
Product defect
tells.tell: "Neutral on its face" plus "business necessity" is the disparate-impact test. Disparate treatment needs intent; disparate impact does not — which is why proxy features in a model are the usual AI exposure.

pairs.dimension: human oversight in the decision loop

a.text: An AI system screens job applicants and produces a ranked shortlist that recruiters hire from.
a.why: Annex III employment use — the system materially influences who gets hired.

b.text: The same system only sorts applicants alphabetically for a recruiter who reads every CV and decides independently.
b.why: Art. 6(3): a narrow procedural task that does not materially influence the outcome falls outside high-risk.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §High-risk AI Systems

pairs.dimension: whose name is on the system

a.text: A bank licenses a third-party high-risk model and uses it internally under the vendor's brand.
a.why: Using a system under another's name keeps you a deployer.

b.text: The same bank puts its own trademark on the system and offers it to customers as its own.
b.why: Placing your name or trademark on a high-risk system makes you its provider, with the full provider obligation set.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers

pairs.dimension: law-enforcement context and real-time vs retrospective

a.text: Police run real-time remote biometric identification across a public square to find suspects generally.
a.why: Art. 5 bans real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, save narrow authorised exceptions.

b.text: Police run the same biometric matching after the fact, on stored footage, under judicial authorisation.
b.why: Post-remote biometric identification is not banned but is Annex III high-risk with authorisation requirements.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §Prohibited AI Systems; §Exceptions to the Biometric Identification Ban

a.text: An employer deploys emotion recognition to monitor staff attentiveness at their desks.
a.why: Art. 5 bans emotion inference in the workplace and in education, outside medical and safety uses.

b.text: A games studio uses emotion recognition in a consumer entertainment app, disclosed to the user.
b.why: Outside workplace and education the ban does not bite; Art. 50 transparency duties apply instead.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §Prohibited AI Systems

a.text: A provider releases a general-purpose model trained well below the systemic-risk compute threshold.
a.why: Baseline duties: technical documentation, information to downstream providers, copyright policy, training-data summary.

b.text: The same provider releases a model whose cumulative training compute exceeds the systemic-risk threshold.
b.why: Adds model evaluation, adversarial testing, systemic-risk assessment and mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity duties.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §Additional Obligations for GPAI with Systemic Risk

pairs.dimension: who the penalty band attaches to

a.text: An organisation deploys a prohibited social-scoring system.
a.why: Breach of the Art. 5 prohibitions attracts the top band.

b.text: An organisation deploys a high-risk system but fails to keep the required technical documentation.
b.why: Non-compliance with obligations other than the Art. 5 prohibitions sits in the middle band.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §Penalties for Non-compliance

a.text: A hospital uses a CE-marked diagnostic AI exactly as the vendor intended.
a.why: Use within the intended purpose leaves provider duties with the vendor.

b.text: The hospital retrains the model on its own data and applies it to a different clinical purpose.
b.why: A substantial modification, or a change of intended purpose that makes a system high-risk, transfers provider obligations to you.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers

a.text: A Dublin firm brings a US-built high-risk system into the EU market for the first time.
a.why: Placing a third-country system on the EU market makes you the importer: verify conformity assessment, CE marking, documentation and the authorised representative.

b.text: A Dublin firm resells that system onward within the EU without altering it.
b.why: Distributors make available a system already on the market; duties are lighter but include checking CE marking and not supplying a system they know to be non-compliant.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §Organizational Context

pairs.dimension: whether the decision is solely automated

a.text: A lender declines a loan automatically on the model score, with no human review.
a.why: A decision based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects triggers Art. 22 safeguards.

b.text: The model flags the application and an underwriter reviews the file and can overturn it.
b.why: Meaningful human involvement with real authority to change the outcome takes it outside "solely" automated. Rubber-stamping does not count.

pairs.citation: Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations in the AI Context

a.text: A system processes facial images specifically to identify a named individual.
a.why: Biometric data processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a person is special-category data.

b.text: A system processes facial images only to count how many people are in a room.
b.why: Without the identification purpose the same raw data is not Art. 9 biometric data, though it remains personal data.

pairs.citation: Ch4 §Understanding the Requirements That Apply to Sensitive or Special Categories of Data

a.text: Customer service transcripts collected to resolve tickets are reused to train a commercial model.
a.why: Training a product on data collected for support is not what the data subject was told; it needs a fresh basis or genuine compatibility analysis.

b.text: The same transcripts are used to audit whether ticket resolution met the stated service standard.
b.why: Quality assurance of the very service the data was collected for is a compatible further purpose.

pairs.citation: Ch4 §Notice, Choice, Consent, and Purpose Limitation in AI

a.text: A model infers users' likely religious beliefs from their posting history.
a.why: Inferring a special category attribute is processing that category, even though it was never collected directly.

b.text: A model records which product pages each user visited.
b.why: Behavioural data alone is personal but not special category, unless it is used to infer a protected attribute.

pairs.citation: Ch4 §Understanding the Requirements That Apply to Sensitive or Special Categories of Data

a.text: A hiring model is deliberately configured to downweight applicants from a protected group.
a.why: Intentional differential treatment on a protected characteristic.

b.text: A hiring model uses postal code, which correlates strongly with race, and rejects one group at a far higher rate.
b.why: Facially neutral feature, disproportionate effect, no intent required. Proxy variables are the classic AI exposure.

pairs.citation: Ch5 §Non-discrimination Laws and AI

a.text: An AI tool screens candidates for a warehouse role and disadvantages older applicants.
a.why: Employment discrimination sits under Title VII, with the ADEA covering age specifically.

b.text: An AI model sets credit limits and produces systematically lower limits for one protected group.
b.why: Credit decisions fall under ECOA, which also requires specific adverse action reasons — hard to give from an opaque model.

pairs.citation: Ch5 §Non-discrimination Laws and AI

pairs.dimension: whether the claim is about capability or about harm caused

a.text: A vendor advertises 99% accuracy for its AI screening tool without evidence.
a.why: Unsubstantiated performance claims are deceptive practices under FTC Act §5.

b.text: A firmware update to an AI home robot causes erratic movement that damages property.
b.why: Defect causing damage is product liability; the EU's revised regime expressly brings software and AI within scope.

pairs.citation: Ch5 §How Consumer Protection Laws Apply to AI; §How Product Liability Laws Apply to AI

pairs.dimension: commercial versus research text and data mining

a.text: A company scrapes news sites commercially where publishers have machine-readably reserved their rights.
a.why: The EU commercial TDM exception can be opted out of by an express reservation, so scraping needs a licence.

b.text: A university mines the same corpus for non-commercial scientific research with lawful access.
b.why: The research TDM exception cannot be overridden by contract or reservation.

pairs.citation: Ch5 §Intellectual Property Laws and AI

a.text: An organisation fails to complete a conformity assessment for a high-risk AI system.
a.why: EU AI Act obligation, enforceable with administrative fines.

b.text: An organisation chooses not to implement the NIST AI RMF's MEASURE function.
b.why: The AI RMF is voluntary guidance. It carries no penalty — though it may inform what counts as reasonable practice.

pairs.citation: Ch7 §NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

a.text: An organisation seeks third-party certification of its AI governance arrangements.
a.why: ISO/IEC 42001 is a management system standard, so it can be audited and certified against.

b.text: An organisation wants agreed definitions of "AI system" and "machine learning" for its policy set.
b.why: ISO/IEC 22989 supplies vocabulary and concepts; there is nothing to certify against.

pairs.citation: Ch7 §ISO Standards

a.text: As the AI Act was originally enacted, when did obligations for standalone Annex III high-risk systems apply?
a.why: The original two-year phase-in date, and what the study guide teaches.

b.text: After the Digital Omnibus agreed in May 2026, when do those same obligations apply?
b.why: The Omnibus deferred standalone Annex III obligations by roughly 16 months. Annex I embedded systems moved to 2 August 2028.

currency.changed: The Digital Omnibus, agreed May 2026, deferred standalone Annex III to 2 December 2027 and Annex I embedded products to 2 August 2028. Most Article 50 transparency duties still apply from 2 August 2026.
currency.exam: BoK v2.1 was approved in September 2025 and predates this. Expect the original timeline unless IAPP has issued an update.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §EU AI Act Implementation

pairs.dimension: who the transparency duty falls on

a.text: A chatbot must be built so that users can tell they are interacting with an AI system.
a.why: Art. 50 places design-time disclosure for AI interaction on the provider.

b.text: An employer using an emotion recognition system must inform the people exposed to it.
b.why: Art. 50 places the duty to inform exposed individuals on the deployer operating the system.

pairs.citation: Ch6 §Limited-risk AI: Targeted Transparency Obligations

a.text: The AI Act lists 8 distinct prohibited AI practices under Article 5 — no specific rule against synthetic intimate imagery.
a.why: The original Article 5 list of 8 practices predates the Amendments Regulation.

b.text: Article 5 prohibits AI systems intended to generate or manipulate non-consensual intimate imagery or CSAM, including systems with inadequate safety guardrails, alongside the original 8 practices.
b.why: The Amendments Regulation adds this ninth prohibited practice, closing a gap the original 8-item list left open.

pairs.citation: EU AI Act Art. 5(1), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(7) (the "Digital Omnibus") — verified against the consolidated text on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng

a.text: A provider whose system meets the Article 6(3) derogation criteria (exempted from high-risk classification) must register it in the EU's public database, providing full supporting information.
a.why: The original Article 6(3)/71 registration duty requires the full information set for these exempted systems.

b.text: An exempted system under Article 6(3) is registered in the EU's public database with a reduced information set.
b.why: The Amendments Regulation keeps the registration duty but reduces the information burden for exempted systems.

pairs.citation: EU AI Act Art. 6(3), Art. 49(2), Annex VIII, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(42) (the "Digital Omnibus") — verified against the consolidated text on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng

a.text: Providers and deployers are required to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff.
a.why: Article 4's original wording is a duty to ensure literacy outright.

b.text: Providers and deployers are required to support the development of AI literacy of their staff.
b.why: The Amendments Regulation softens Article 4 from an 'ensure' duty to a 'support the development of' duty.

pairs.citation: EU AI Act Art. 4, as replaced by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(5) (the "Digital Omnibus") — verified against the consolidated text on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng

pairs.dimension: processing sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction

a.text: Only high-risk AI system providers may process sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction, and only when strictly necessary with safeguards in place.
a.why: The original Article 10(5) scope is limited to high-risk AI system providers.

b.text: Providers and deployers of other AI systems and GPAI models, and deployers of high-risk AI systems, may process sensitive personal data for bias detection and correction when strictly necessary with safeguards in place.
b.why: The Amendments Regulation widens Article 10(5)'s scope beyond just high-risk providers, while keeping the strict-necessity/safeguards test unchanged.

pairs.citation: EU AI Act Art. 10(5) (original limits) and new Art. 4a, inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(6) (the "Digital Omnibus") — verified against the consolidated text on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng

pairs.dimension: European AI Office's regulatory powers over GPAI-based systems

a.text: The European AI Office and member state regulators have overlapping regulatory powers for AI systems built on GPAI models, where the same provider developed both the model and the system.
a.why: The original allocation of powers between the AI Office and national regulators is overlapping, not exclusive.

b.text: The European AI Office has exclusive competence over AI systems built on GPAI models where the same provider developed both — except for high-risk systems under Annex I and specific Annex III categories such as critical infrastructure and law enforcement.
b.why: The Amendments Regulation moves the AI Office from overlapping to exclusive competence for this category, carving out Annex I and specific Annex III high-risk systems.

pairs.citation: EU AI Act Art. 75(1), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(31) (the "Digital Omnibus") — verified against the consolidated text on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng

pairs.dimension: proportionality of penalties for small mid-cap (SMC) enterprises

a.text: Enforcement penalties are capped for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), but small mid-cap (SMC) enterprises get no such cap.
a.why: The original penalty regime's proportionality cap applies to SMEs only.

b.text: SMEs and SMCs pay the lower of the percentage of global annual turnover or the fixed amount, while larger organisations pay the higher value.
b.why: The Amendments Regulation extends the SME proportionality cap to SMCs on the same lower-of-two-values basis.

pairs.citation: EU AI Act Art. 99(6a), inserted by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(38) (the "Digital Omnibus") — verified against the consolidated text on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng

pairs.dimension: high-risk AI systems regulated by the EU Machinery Regulation

a.text: AI systems that are products, or safety components of products, regulated by the EU Machinery Regulation must directly adhere to the AI Act's high-risk AI system requirements.
a.why: In the original Annex I, the Machinery Regulation sits in Section A, which triggers direct high-risk AI Act requirements.

b.text: The Machinery Regulation sits in Annex I Section B, so the AI Act's high-risk AI system requirements do not apply to it directly.
b.why: The Amendments Regulation reclassifies the Machinery Regulation into Annex I Section B, removing the direct high-risk trigger.

pairs.citation: EU AI Act Annex I, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 Art. 1(41) — point 1 of Section A deleted, Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 added to Section B (the "Digital Omnibus") — verified against the consolidated text on eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng

pairs.dimension: shared vocabulary vs certifiable management system

a.text: Defines the common vocabulary and conceptual framework for AI — terms like AI system, machine learning, training, inference, and bias — so every other AI standard rests on the same definitions.
a.why: This is the dictionary of AI governance: it eliminates ambiguity in technical, legal, and governance discussions by fixing what the words mean, but it imposes no organisational requirements of its own.

b.text: Specifies a certifiable AI management system (AIMS) — policies, governance structures, risk controls, and oversight mechanisms an organisation can be independently audited against.
b.why: Published 2023, this moves AI governance from voluntary principles to auditable, certifiable practice — the AI-governance equivalent of ISO/IEC 27001 for information security.

pairs.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.D ISO Core AI Standards (SG)

pairs.dimension: assessing effects on people/society vs guiding organisational risk management

a.text: Guides how an organisation assesses an AI system's effects on individuals and societies — an AI impact assessment standard.
a.why: 42005 scopes the assessment around the people and communities the system touches, not the organisation's internal risk posture.

b.text: Guides how an organisation manages AI-related risk across its own processes — risk identification, analysis, evaluation, and treatment.
b.why: 23894 is the AI-specific companion to ISO 31000's generic risk-management process, aimed at the organisation's risk function rather than the affected individual.

pairs.citation: ISO/IEC 42005:2025, Information technology — Artificial intelligence — AI system impact assessment, iso.org/standard/42005 (published April 2025; verified 2026-08-02). ISO/IEC 23894:2023, Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Guidance on risk management, iso.org/standard/77304 (verified 2026-08-02); also per AIGP Study Guide §II.D (SG).

a.text: A marketing bot's ad copy claims the AI hiring tool is 'completely objective'; the system later exhibits bias and the regulator calls the claim deceptive.
a.why: The FTC Act bars false or exaggerated claims about what a product can do — the defect here is in what was said about the system, not in the system itself.

b.text: A flaw in how the system was engineered means it fails to perform as safely as consumers are entitled to expect, and a user is injured as a result.
b.why: Under doctrines like the EU Product Liability Directive, manufacturers can be strictly liable for a defective design even without proof of negligence — the harm traces to engineering, not messaging.

pairs.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.B Consumer Protection Laws / Product Liability and Safety Laws (SG)

a.text: Widely adopted, high-level principles for trustworthy AI — a values-level reference point rather than a step-by-step process.
a.why: The OECD's contribution is normative and international: what trustworthy AI should look like, not how to operationalise finding and fixing its risks.

b.text: A U.S.-originated but globally influential framework built specifically to help organisations identify and mitigate AI risks in practice.
b.why: The RMF is operational scaffolding — functions like Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage — that an organisation actually runs, distinct from OECD's principle-level guidance.

pairs.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.D Industry Standards and Tools (SG)

pairs.dimension: what the tool records — model facts vs anticipated harms

a.text: A published summary of a model's data sources, known risks, and mitigations, written in language a non-expert can understand.
a.why: A model card documents what the model already is and does — transparency about a finished artefact.

b.text: A structured exercise, run before deployment, to anticipate and manage the potential risks and harms an AI system could cause.
b.why: An impact assessment looks forward at consequences for people and society, not backward at what the model card already discloses about the artefact.

pairs.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.D Industry Standards and Tools (SG)

pairs.dimension: assurance of quality vs shifting the cost of a claim

a.text: The vendor contractually promises the AI model will perform to a stated standard; if it doesn't, the deployer has a contract remedy against the vendor.
a.why: A warranty is a promise about the product itself — it fails or holds based on whether the system performs as stated.

b.text: The vendor agrees to cover the deployer's losses if a third party sues over IP infringement or a regulatory violation caused by the model — but the clause is voided once the deployer uses the model outside the jurisdictions the vendor covered.
b.why: Indemnity reallocates who pays for a third-party claim; it says nothing about whether the model itself works, and — as exam-prep materials note — it can be voided by deploying outside the covered jurisdiction.

pairs.citation: AIGP Study Guide §IV.B Vendor Contractual Terms (SG, l.887)

a.text: A claimant must show the developer failed to exercise reasonable care in designing, testing, or validating the system before liability attaches.
a.why: Negligence liability turns on proving a failure of care — no proof of fault, no claim.

b.text: Under the EU Product Liability Directive, a manufacturer can be held liable for damage caused by a defective AI-enabled product even without any proof of negligence.
b.why: Strict liability removes the fault question entirely: if the product was defective and caused harm, liability can attach regardless of how carefully the manufacturer behaved.

pairs.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.B Product Liability and Safety Laws (SG)

pairs.dimension: sector-specific duty — patient privacy vs credit-decision transparency

a.text: An AI diagnostic tool that processes protected health information must comply with privacy and security rules covering access controls, audit logs, and breach notification.
a.why: HIPAA's obligations attach the moment protected health information is processed, regardless of whether a decision is even automated.

b.text: An AI model that denies a consumer a loan must provide an adverse-action notice explaining the key factors driving the decision, and the underlying credit-scoring model must not produce discriminatory outcomes.
b.why: These finance-sector laws require explainability and non-discrimination specifically for credit decisions — a different duty, in a different sector, from HIPAA's data-handling rules.

pairs.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.B Sector-Specific Regulations — Healthcare (SG), Finance (SG, l.1279)

steps.detail: Up to €35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

steps.detail: Up to €15 million or 3% — provider and deployer duties, notified body and transparency obligations.

steps.detail: Transparency duties for AI interaction, synthetic content, deepfakes and emotion recognition. Unchanged by the Omnibus.

steps.label: High-risk: Annex I embedded products

timeline.title: Global Obligations Timeline

timeline.note: Jurisdictions marked scope "horizon" are professional currency rather than blueprint content; they are excluded from mastery scoring. "Ongoing / uncertain" covers proposed bills and rolling state/regional developments with no confirmed date.

Article 50 transparency (chatbot disclosure, synthetic-content marking, deepfake labelling) enforceable now

Extraterritorial where output is used in the EU

Unfair and deceptive practices enforcement over AI claims
Existing anti-discrimination law applies to AI decisions
Sector regulators act within existing authority

Notice duties for AI use in employment

jurisdictions.name: Texas

Intent-based prohibitions
Regulatory sandbox

jurisdictions.name: New York City

Published audit summary
Candidate notice

Provenance disclosure for large generative systems

LGPD applies to personal data in the meantime

Cross-sector principles delivered through existing regulators
UK GDPR continues to apply

Binding AI requirements apply to Commonwealth agencies only (from 2026-06-15)

Binds States Parties, not companies directly

National implementation decides how far the private sector is reached
jurisdictions.tell: International instrument, not a national law — in force and binding, but on states: companies feel it only through national implementation.

jurisdictions.name: Singapore
instruments: Model AI Governance Framework (+ GenAI edition 2024)
Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (2026-01-22)
obligations: No binding AI-specific statute
Frameworks address developers, deployers and agent operators — all non-binding
AI Verify process checks and technical tests for AI assurance
Sector regulators issue AI guidance under existing binding law (PDPA, MAS FEAT)

jurisdictions.name: Taiwan

No operational obligations or penalties on private business yet
MODA must build a risk-classification framework; sector rules to follow
Implementing measures due within 24 months of effectiveness

Transparency, security and audit duties

Existing technology-neutral law applies (FADP, product, sectoral finance/medical rules)
CoE Convention implementation bill in drafting

jurisdictions.tell: The deliberate minimalist — a lean, sector-specific approach chosen on purpose, next door to the EU's comprehensive regime.

Binds those who provide and those who deploy such systems, in data-protection roles

Commissioner-licensing model with risk rules and penalties, if enacted

cards.q: From 2 December 2027, your CV-screening system sits in the EU high-risk tier and you want it on the EU market under your own brand. Which route completes first?
options: An internal-control conformity assessment against the requirements, then CE marking and registration in the EU database
A notified-body (third-party) conformity assessment, mandatory for every high-risk system
A fundamental rights impact assessment carried out by the end customer
An annual independent bias audit with a published summary
cards.answer: An internal-control conformity assessment against the requirements, then CE marking and registration in the EU database
cards.why: Annex III employment systems use the internal-control route (Art. 43(2)) — self-assess, CE-mark, register. Nearest confusable: (b) third-party assessment is for biometrics without fully applied harmonised standards. (c) is the deployer's FRIA; (d) is NYC LL144. High-risk duties bind from 2027-12-02 (Digital Omnibus deferral), which is why the stem is future-dated.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Classification Requirements; EU AI Act Art. 43(2); Council 2026-06-29 Omnibus adoption

cards.q: It is 2 August 2026 and you provide a general-purpose AI model on the EU market. Which statement about your position is accurate?
options: Your GPAI obligations have applied since August 2025, and from today the Commission can fine you up to 3% of global turnover or €15M
GPAI obligations only start today, together with the fining powers
You face the 7% / €35M band reserved for the gravest infringements
Nothing binds you until the high-risk regime applies in December 2027
cards.answer: Your GPAI obligations have applied since August 2025, and from today the Commission can fine you up to 3% of global turnover or €15M
cards.why: The stagger is the tested point and (b) is the nearest confusable: Art. 53 duties applied from 2025-08-02, while the Commission/AI Office enforcement and fining powers (Art. 101) arrive 2026-08-02. (c) is the prohibited-practices band, not the GPAI band; (d) confuses the GPAI chapter with the Annex III deferral.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Requirements for General-purpose AI; EU AI Act Art. 101; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: Your company provides a public generative service producing synthetic images, plus a consumer chatbot, in the EU. As of today, what does Article 50 require of you as provider?
options: Mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable way and design the chatbot so users know they are interacting with an AI system
Label each deepfake you publish and inform people exposed to emotion recognition
Nothing yet — the transparency rules were deferred to December 2027 with the rest of the Act
Complete a conformity assessment and affix CE marking to the service
cards.answer: Mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable way and design the chatbot so users know they are interacting with an AI system
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): deepfake labelling and emotion-recognition disclosure are the DEPLOYER'S Article 50 duties; the provider side is machine-readable marking plus interaction disclosure. (c) misreads the Omnibus — Article 50 became enforceable 2026-08-02 (only a watermarking grace to 2026-12-02 for systems already on the market); (d) is high-risk product machinery, not transparency.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Limited-risk AI: Targeted Transparency Obligations; EU AI Act Art. 50; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: You are pitching an EU launch of a workplace tool that scores employees' emotional state from webcam feeds to flag 'disengagement'. What is its status under the AI Act today?
options: It cannot be marketed — emotion inference in the workplace has been outlawed since February 2025, save narrow medical and safety exceptions
High-risk — permitted once a conformity assessment is completed
Limited-risk — a transparency notice to staff suffices
Unregulated until December 2027
cards.answer: It cannot be marketed — emotion inference in the workplace has been outlawed since February 2025, save narrow medical and safety exceptions
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): emotion recognition OUTSIDE workplaces and schools sits in Annex III as high-risk, but in the workplace it is an Article 5 prohibited practice — no conformity route legalises it. (d) misapplies the Omnibus: the deferral touched Annex III, while the prohibitions have applied since 2025-02-02.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Prohibited AI Systems; EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(f)

cards.q: Your frontier model is classified as GPAI with systemic risk. A safety failure causes a serious incident. What is your reporting position today?
options: Track, document and report the incident and corrective measures to the AI Office without undue delay — a duty live since August 2025
Report to national market surveillance authorities under the high-risk regime, a duty that binds from December 2027
No AI Act duty — incident reporting only arrives with the Annex III regime
Publish the incident in the EU database within 72 hours
cards.answer: Track, document and report the incident and corrective measures to the AI Office without undue delay — a duty live since August 2025
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): Article 73 serious-incident reporting attaches to HIGH-RISK systems and was deferred with Annex III to 2027-12-02; the systemic-risk GPAI duty (Art. 55, to the AI Office) has applied since 2025-08-02. (d) grafts the GDPR's 72-hour breach idiom onto the wrong instrument.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Additional Obligations for GPAI with Systemic Risk; EU AI Act Art. 55; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: From 2 December 2027 your firm will run a vendor's CE-marked CV-screening system on EU hiring. Which duty set lands on you?
options: Use per the provider's instructions, assign trained human oversight, ensure relevant input data, monitor operation and keep the generated logs
Draw up the technical documentation and run the conformity assessment
Register the system in the EU database as its provider
Mark the system's outputs as artificially generated
cards.answer: Use per the provider's instructions, assign trained human oversight, ensure relevant input data, monitor operation and keep the generated logs
cards.why: Article 26 is the deployer's operational set. Nearest confusables: (b) and (c) are the PROVIDER'S pre-market duties — the deployer inherits neither by merely using the system; (d) is the Article 50 synthetic-content marking duty, which belongs to providers of generative systems.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Shared and Overlapping Responsibilities; EU AI Act Art. 26; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: From December 2027, which EU deployer must complete a fundamental rights impact assessment before first using a high-risk system — and when?
options: A public body or private operator of public services (plus banks and insurers for certain systems), once before first use
Every deployer of any high-risk system, annually
The provider, before placing the system on the market
Any controller processing high-risk personal data, before processing begins
cards.answer: A public body or private operator of public services (plus banks and insurers for certain systems), once before first use
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (d): that describes the GDPR Article 35 DPIA. The Article 27 FRIA is deployer-side and limited to public-sector-type deployers plus specified credit/insurance uses — not every deployer, and not annual (b); (c) confuses it with the provider's conformity assessment.
cards.citation: Ch6 §High-risk AI Systems; EU AI Act Art. 27; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: Your marketing team runs AI-generated video of a photorealistic presenter indistinguishable from a real person in EU campaigns, and your retail unit uses a system inferring shoppers' emotions in stores. As deployer, what must you disclose today?
options: Label the video as artificially generated and inform shoppers they are exposed to emotion recognition — both duties are live now
Nothing until December 2027, when the transparency chapter applies
Only machine-readable watermarking, which is the provider's task anyway
A fundamental rights impact assessment for both uses
cards.answer: Label the video as artificially generated and inform shoppers they are exposed to emotion recognition — both duties are live now
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the Omnibus deferred Annex III high-risk duties, not Article 50, which became enforceable 2026-08-02. (c) names the PROVIDER'S marking duty — the deployer side is deepfake labelling and informing exposed persons; (d) the FRIA is a high-risk instrument for public-sector-type deployers, not a transparency disclosure.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Limited-risk AI: Targeted Transparency Obligations; EU AI Act Art. 50(3)-(4); Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: From December 2027, what will 'human oversight' concretely require of a deployer running a high-risk system?
options: Assigning it to natural persons with the competence, training and authority to intervene
Designing the system so it can be effectively overseen, with built-in operational constraints
Having a human approve every individual output before it takes effect
Notifying the market surveillance authority of the oversight arrangements
cards.answer: Assigning it to natural persons with the competence, training and authority to intervene
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): enabling oversight by design is the PROVIDER'S Article 14 duty; the deployer's Article 26(2) duty is assigning capable people. (c) overstates — oversight means meaningful ability to intervene, not per-output human approval.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Human Oversight; EU AI Act Arts. 14, 26(2); Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: From 2 December 2027 your Dublin entity will bring a US developer's high-risk system, sold under the US brand, into the EU market. Before you do, what must you check?
options: That the conformity assessment was carried out, technical documentation exists and the system bears CE marking — then add your own name and contact details
Nothing — the US developer retains all duties as provider
You must run your own conformity assessment and re-register the system
That the developer appointed you as its authorised representative
cards.answer: That the conformity assessment was carried out, technical documentation exists and the system bears CE marking — then add your own name and contact details
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c): the importer VERIFIES the provider completed the pre-market steps (Art. 23) — it does not redo them. (d) confuses the importer with the authorised representative, a separate mandated role; (b) ignores that importers carry their own verification and identification duties.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Mapping Your Role in the AI Lifecycle; EU AI Act Art. 23 (cf. Art. 24 distributors); Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: Your import business starts selling that third-country high-risk system under its own trademark instead of the developer's. What happens to your obligations?
options: You are now treated as the provider and assume the provider's duties, including conformity obligations
You remain an importer — branding does not change the role analysis
You become a distributor with only storage-and-transport care duties
You and the original developer share provider duties equally
cards.answer: You are now treated as the provider and assume the provider's duties, including conformity obligations
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): putting your name or trademark on a high-risk system already on the market is precisely the Article 25(1)(a) trigger that re-allocates the provider role. (d) is wrong on the mechanism — the original provider owes cooperation and documentation handover, not joint provider status.
cards.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers; EU AI Act Art. 25(1)(a)

cards.q: A non-EU provider wants an EU foothold for its high-risk system. It signs a written mandate with a Paris firm to keep documentation available and cooperate with authorities, while a Madrid company physically places the system on the EU market. Which is which?
options: Paris is the authorised representative; Madrid is the importer
Paris is the importer; Madrid is the distributor
Both are importers — the first EU entity in the chain takes the role
Paris is a deployer acting on the provider's behalf
cards.answer: Paris is the authorised representative; Madrid is the importer
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the WRITTEN MANDATE to act for a third-country provider is the defining mark of the authorised representative (Art. 22), while the importer is the EU entity that places a third-country system on the market. Neither role attaches by mere position in the chain (c), and neither firm is using the system (d).
cards.citation: Ch6 §Mapping Your Role in the AI Lifecycle; EU AI Act Art. 22

cards.q: The AI Office opens an inquiry into your GPAI model and requests documentation. What do you produce?
options: The Article 53 technical documentation, information for downstream providers, your copyright policy and the public training-data summary
The EU declaration of conformity and CE-marking file
A fundamental rights impact assessment
Nothing — GPAI documentation duties only bind from December 2027
cards.answer: The Article 53 technical documentation, information for downstream providers, your copyright policy and the public training-data summary
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): declarations of conformity and CE marking belong to the HIGH-RISK product-safety machinery, not the GPAI chapter. (c) is a deployer instrument; (d) misapplies the Omnibus deferral, which moved Annex III/I dates and left GPAI duties (applying since 2025-08-02) untouched.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Requirements for General-purpose AI; EU AI Act Art. 53

cards.q: A market surveillance authority probes your EU operation: you have been scraping social-media photos at scale to grow a face-recognition database. What is the correct read of your position?
options: The practice has been unlawful outright since February 2025 — wind it down; exposure sits in the top fining band
It is high-risk: complete a conformity assessment and you may continue
It is lawful until the biometric provisions apply in December 2027
cards.answer: The practice has been unlawful outright since February 2025 — wind it down; exposure sits in the top fining band
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): untargeted scraping of facial images is an Article 5 PROHIBITED practice, not an Annex III high-risk use — no conformity route legalises it. (c) fails on currency: the prohibitions applied from 2025-02-02 and were untouched by the Digital Omnibus.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Prohibited AI Systems; EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(e)

cards.q: Your EU compliance calendar flags 2 December 2026. What actually lands on that date?
options: The watermarking grace for systems already on the market before August 2026 ends, and the new prohibition on AI generating NCII/CSAM starts to apply
The Annex III high-risk obligations become enforceable
GPAI fining powers take effect
Nothing — the next AI Act milestone is December 2027
cards.answer: The watermarking grace for systems already on the market before August 2026 ends, and the new prohibition on AI generating NCII/CSAM starts to apply
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): Annex III sits a full year later, on 2027-12-02 — 2026-12-02 is the Omnibus's own transition date, closing the Art. 50 watermarking grace for pre-August-2026 systems and switching on the new Art. 5 NCII/CSAM ban it added. (c) is stale by four months — fining powers arrived 2026-08-02; (d) misses both December-2026 items.
cards.citation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus) — transition dates

cards.q: Your board asks which EU AI Act duties bind the company today, 2 August 2026. The accurate briefing is:
options: Prohibitions and AI literacy; GPAI duties, now backed by fining powers; Article 50 transparency; and every member state must have a sandbox — the high-risk regime is not among them
The full Act, including Annex III high-risk conformity assessment
Only the prohibitions — everything else was deferred
Nothing — the Act as a whole applies from December 2027
cards.answer: Prohibitions and AI literacy; GPAI duties, now backed by fining powers; Article 50 transparency; and every member state must have a sandbox — the high-risk regime is not among them
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the pre-Omnibus calendar would indeed have made high-risk duties bite today, but Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved Annex III to 2027-12-02. (c) over-corrects in the other direction — GPAI duties and Article 50 are live alongside the prohibitions.
cards.citation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus); Council 2026-06-29 Omnibus adoption

cards.q: You want to trial a novel EU offering with supervisory cover before the high-risk regime bites. What is actually available to you today?
options: A national AI regulatory sandbox — every member state must have at least one operational as of 2 August 2026
Nothing yet — sandboxes arrive with the high-risk regime in December 2027
The UK's proposed AI Growth Labs, which cover EU launches too
cards.answer: A national AI regulatory sandbox — every member state must have at least one operational as of 2 August 2026
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the Digital Omnibus moved the Annex III date but left the Article 57 sandbox deadline at 2026-08-02. (c) confuses the UK's Regulating for Growth Bill — a proposal before Parliament, and not EU law — with the EU member-state obligation.
cards.citation: EU AI Act Art. 57; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus)

cards.q: Your firm expands into the UK. Who will actually apply the five cross-sector AI principles to your business?
options: Existing sectoral regulators — the ICO, FCA, Ofcom and peers — each within its own statutory remit
A dedicated central AI regulator created for the purpose
DSIT, which enforces the principles directly against firms
No one — the principles have no supervisory owner
cards.answer: Existing sectoral regulators — the ICO, FCA, Ofcom and peers — each within its own statutory remit
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the UK deliberately created no central AI regulator — the principles route through existing sectoral remits, so one AI system can face the ICO on data, the FCA on financial services and Ofcom on content. DSIT (c) coordinates policy and steers the framework; it does not enforce against firms. (d) understates: regulators apply the principles through their existing statutory powers.
cards.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.C UK pro-innovation approach; DSIT Blueprint for AI regulation (Oct 2025)

cards.q: Since 5 February 2026, when can your UK operation take a significant, solely automated decision about a customer?
options: Generally yes, with safeguards — unless special-category data is involved, where the stricter regime persists
Never without explicit consent, under a general restriction on automated decisions
Freely — the UK abolished all automated-decision rules
Only after completing an EU-style conformity assessment
cards.answer: Generally yes, with safeguards — unless special-category data is involved, where the stricter regime persists
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): that is the OLD Article 22 posture the Data (Use and Access) Act replaced — UK GDPR Articles 22A–22D flip the default to permission-with-safeguards (human intervention, representations, contest). (c) overshoots: safeguards and the special-category carve-out remain; (d) imports the wrong regime entirely.
cards.citation: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80 (UK GDPR Arts. 22A–22D, in force 2026-02-05)

cards.q: What did SI 2026/425, in force 12 May 2026, change about UK AI supervision?
options: It placed the ICO under a statutory duty to produce a code of practice on AI and automated decision-making, including a children's-data component
It gave the UK its first binding AI statute for companies
It transposed the EU AI Act into UK law
It created a mandatory licensing regime for AI developers
cards.answer: It placed the ICO under a statutory duty to produce a code of practice on AI and automated decision-making, including a children's-data component
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the binding duty falls on the REGULATOR — to prepare the code — not directly on companies; the code will then guide enforcement of existing law. (c) is impossible post-Brexit mechanics; nothing in the SI licenses developers (d).
cards.citation: SI 2026/425 (DPA 2018 s.124A AI code duty, in force 2026-05-12)

cards.q: How does the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI reach your UK business?
options: Indirectly — the UK has been a party since November 2025, but the treaty binds the state, so you feel it only through domestic implementation
Directly — treaty obligations apply to companies operating in ratifying states
Not at all — the UK signed but never ratified
Through the EU, which enforces it in the UK
cards.answer: Indirectly — the UK has been a party since November 2025, but the treaty binds the state, so you feel it only through domestic implementation
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): CETS 225 binds States Parties, not firms. (c) describes SWITZERLAND'S position (signed 2025-03-27, not ratified) — the UK ratified, and the Convention has been in force for it since 2025-11-01. (d) is doubly wrong: the UK left the EU and the EU's own accession takes effect only from 2026-09-01.
cards.citation: CoE Framework Convention CETS 225 (in force 2025-11-01; UK a party)

cards.q: The Regulating for Growth Bill announced in the May 2026 King's Speech would give the UK…
options: Cross-economy AI sandbox powers ('AI Growth Labs') and statutory backing for AISI — but it is still a proposal before Parliament
An EU-style AI Act with risk tiers
Binding duties already in force since May 2026
A statutory duty on the ICO to write an AI code
cards.answer: Cross-economy AI sandbox powers ('AI Growth Labs') and statutory backing for AISI — but it is still a proposal before Parliament
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c): a King's Speech announcement is not law — the Bill remains before Parliament. (d) is the SEPARATE SI 2026/425, which IS in force; (b) is what the Bill deliberately is not — the UK is legislating for sandboxes, not for an AI Act.
cards.citation: King's Speech 2026-05-13 — Regulating for Growth Bill (proposed)

cards.q: Which set are the UK's cross-sector AI principles that regulators apply?
options: Safety, security and robustness; appropriate transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress
GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE
Human agency, technical robustness, privacy, transparency, diversity, societal wellbeing, accountability
Unacceptable, high, limited and minimal risk tiers
cards.answer: Safety, security and robustness; appropriate transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c): those are the EU HLEG trustworthy-AI requirements, not the UK's five pro-innovation principles. (b) is the NIST AI RMF's four functions; (d) is the EU AI Act's risk classification — a tiering scheme, not a principles set.
cards.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.C UK pro-innovation approach (five cross-sector principles)

cards.q: A client asks: 'Surely the UK has its own AI Act by now?' The correct answer is:
options: No — the October 2025 Blueprint confirmed the regulator-led route, and the anticipated AI Bill never materialised
Yes — the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 is the UK's AI Act
Yes — the Regulating for Growth Bill became law in May 2026
cards.answer: No — the October 2025 Blueprint confirmed the regulator-led route, and the anticipated AI Bill never materialised
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the DUAA is data-protection law that happens to reshape automated-decision rules — it is not an AI statute. (c) fails on status: the Regulating for Growth Bill was only ANNOUNCED in the King's Speech and remains before Parliament.
cards.citation: DSIT Blueprint for AI regulation (Oct 2025); House of Commons Library — AI regulation in the UK

cards.q: After the DUAA reforms, how does the UK's treatment of solely automated significant decisions compare with EU GDPR Article 22?
options: They diverged on 5 February 2026 — the EU keeps the restriction model, while the UK switched to a permit-with-safeguards model
They remain aligned — the EU made an equivalent amendment at the same time
The divergence runs the other way — the UK now restricts what the EU permits
cards.answer: They diverged on 5 February 2026 — the EU keeps the restriction model, while the UK switched to a permit-with-safeguards model
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c), the direction-of-travel reversal — easy if you anchor on the shared pre-Brexit text: it is the UK that liberalised, while EU Article 22 keeps its restriction-shaped default. (b) fails because the EU has made no equivalent amendment — this is now a live cross-border compliance split for any group running one decisioning stack in both markets.
cards.citation: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 s.80 (UK GDPR Arts. 22A–22D); AIGP Study Guide §II.A automated decision-making

cards.q: Your compliance lead asks whether the Council of Europe Framework Convention adds items to your company's obligations register. Correct answer:
options: Not directly — it binds States Parties, covering public authorities and private actors acting for them; each party chooses how to reach the wider private sector
Yes — it imposes conformity assessment duties on providers
Yes — any company in a ratifying state must register its AI systems with the Council of Europe
No, because the Convention is not yet in force
cards.answer: Not directly — it binds States Parties, covering public authorities and private actors acting for them; each party chooses how to reach the wider private sector
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): conformity assessment is EU AI Act machinery — the Convention contains no company-facing operative rules. (d) is the stale fact this game punishes: CETS 225 entered into force on 2025-11-01.
cards.citation: CoE Framework Convention CETS 225 (in force 2025-11-01)

cards.q: What distinction does CETS No. 225 hold in the history of AI governance?
options: The first binding international AI treaty — in force since 1 November 2025 after its fifth ratification
The first national AI statute
A non-binding declaration, like the OECD AI Principles
An EU regulation with direct effect in member states
cards.answer: The first binding international AI treaty — in force since 1 November 2025 after its fifth ratification
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c): unlike the OECD Principles or the G7 Hiroshima Process, CETS 225 creates binding obligations for its parties. It is a Council of Europe treaty open to non-members — international, not national (b) — and not an EU act (d): the EU is acceding to it as a party.
cards.citation: CoE Framework Convention CETS 225 (in force 2025-11-01; ratifiers incl. UK, France, Norway)

cards.q: When does the Framework Convention start applying to the EU itself?
options: 1 September 2026 — the EU ratified on 15 May 2026 and the Convention takes effect for it from that later date
It already has, since the Convention entered into force in November 2025
Never — the EU cannot join a Council of Europe treaty
2 December 2027, aligned with the AI Act's high-risk regime
cards.answer: 1 September 2026 — the EU ratified on 15 May 2026 and the Convention takes effect for it from that later date
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the treaty's general entry into force (2025-11-01) bound the states that had ratified by then — for each new party, including the EU, the clock runs from its own ratification, with effect 2026-09-01. (d) borrows the Digital Omnibus deferral date from an entirely different instrument.
cards.citation: CoE — EU ratifies the Framework Convention on AI (2026-05-15; effective 2026-09-01)

cards.q: The Council of Europe's HUDERIA is best described as:
options: Non-binding guidance for assessing AI risks and impacts on human rights, democracy and the rule of law
The mandatory impact assessment every Convention party must impose on companies
The EU AI Act's fundamental rights impact assessment
A certifiable management-system standard
cards.answer: Non-binding guidance for assessing AI risks and impacts on human rights, democracy and the rule of law
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c): the FRIA (AI Act Art. 27) is EU law and deployer-facing — HUDERIA is Council of Europe methodology supporting Convention implementation, and it is guidance, not itself mandatory (b). (d) describes ISO/IEC 42001, a different animal entirely.
cards.citation: CoE CAI — HUDERIA risk and impact assessment methodology (2024)

cards.q: What does the Framework Convention's signature list tell you about its reach?
options: Around 46 signatories by May 2026 — including non-European states such as the US, Canada and Japan — but signature alone does not bind; ratification does
Only Council of Europe member states may sign
Every signatory is immediately bound from the moment of signature
The US has ratified and is fully bound
cards.answer: Around 46 signatories by May 2026 — including non-European states such as the US, Canada and Japan — but signature alone does not bind; ratification does
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c): signature signals intent — obligations attach only on ratification and entry into force for that party. The US and Japan have signed but not ratified (d), and the treaty is expressly open to non-members (b).
cards.citation: CoE Framework Convention CETS 225 — signature/ratification status (46 signatories, May 2026)

cards.q: Your company opens a Zurich office. What AI-specific law applies to your Swiss operations today?
options: None — Switzerland deliberately chose a lean, sector-specific approach; a draft bill is only due for consultation by end-2026
The EU AI Act, which applies in Switzerland via the bilateral agreements
A Swiss horizontal AI statute in force since 2025
The CoE Convention, which Switzerland has ratified and implemented
cards.answer: None — Switzerland deliberately chose a lean, sector-specific approach; a draft bill is only due for consultation by end-2026
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): Switzerland is neither EU nor EEA, so the AI Act is not Swiss law — though it can still reach a Swiss firm extraterritorially when output is used in the EU. (d) fails on status: Switzerland SIGNED the Convention in March 2025 but has not ratified it.
cards.citation: Swiss Federal Council AI decision (Feb 2025); White & Case AI Watch — Switzerland

cards.q: Where does Switzerland stand on the Council of Europe Framework Convention?
options: Signed in March 2025, not yet ratified — the implementing bill is in drafting, with public consultation planned by end-2026
Ratified — in force for Switzerland since November 2025
Not signed — Switzerland stays outside all international AI instruments
Signed, and directly applicable without any implementing law
cards.answer: Signed in March 2025, not yet ratified — the implementing bill is in drafting, with public consultation planned by end-2026
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): that is the UNITED KINGDOM'S position — the UK ratified and the Convention has been in force for it since 2025-11-01. Switzerland is a signatory only, and a treaty of this kind needs ratification plus implementing legislation before it binds (contra d).
cards.citation: Swiss Federal Council — CoE Convention signed 2025-03-27, ratification planned; consultation due end-2026

cards.q: What did the Swiss Federal Council actually decide in February 2025 about regulating AI?
options: Implement the CoE Convention mainly for state actors, add cross-sectoral rules only where fundamental rights demand, and otherwise rely on sectoral and non-binding measures
Draft an EU-style horizontal AI act
Suspend high-risk AI deployments pending legislation
Join the EU AI Act regime as an EEA-style partner
cards.answer: Implement the CoE Convention mainly for state actors, add cross-sectoral rules only where fundamental rights demand, and otherwise rely on sectoral and non-binding measures
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the decision expressly REJECTED a horizontal act in favour of the lean sectoral route — the opposite of the EU's choice next door. (d) mistakes Switzerland's institutional position: it is not in the EEA and has no mechanism to adopt the AI Act wholesale.
cards.citation: Swiss Federal Council AI decision (2025-02-12): sectoral approach, CoE implementation

cards.q: With no AI statute on the books, what governs an AI-driven credit product in Switzerland today?
options: Existing technology-neutral law — the Federal Act on Data Protection plus sectoral finance rules
Nothing, until the AI bill passes
The EU AI Act's credit-scoring rules, applied directly by the Swiss financial regulator
cards.answer: Existing technology-neutral law — the Federal Act on Data Protection plus sectoral finance rules
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b), the classic 'no AI law means no law' error — the FADP, product rules and financial supervision all reach AI systems today. (c) is wrong on mechanism: EU rules are not Swiss law and bite only extraterritorially where output is used in the EU market.
cards.citation: Swiss Federal Council AI decision (Feb 2025); Chambers — Artificial Intelligence 2026: Switzerland

cards.q: A distributor takes a high-risk system already on the EU market and starts selling it under its own name. Under the AI Act's role rules, the distributor…
options: Is treated as the provider and assumes the provider's obligations
Remains a distributor, since it did not modify the system
Becomes an importer
Shares liability 50/50 with the original provider
cards.answer: Is treated as the provider and assumes the provider's obligations
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): modification is a SEPARATE trigger (Art. 25(1)(b)) — name-or-trademark substitution alone re-allocates the provider role under Art. 25(1)(a). (c) mistakes the supply-chain geography test for the branding test; (d) invents a sharing rule the Act does not contain.
cards.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers; EU AI Act Art. 25(1)(a)

cards.q: A hospital rewires a CE-marked diagnostic system's model to change how it scores patients — a substantial modification — and keeps using it internally. What follows?
options: The hospital becomes the provider of the modified system and owes a fresh conformity assessment
It stays a deployer, because it never sells the system to anyone
The original vendor remains solely responsible for the system
cards.answer: The hospital becomes the provider of the modified system and owes a fresh conformity assessment
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): putting a substantially modified high-risk system INTO SERVICE under your own authority triggers the Art. 25(1)(b) shift even without a sale. (c) is wrong on the residue — the original provider owes cooperation and documentation handover, not responsibility for someone else's modification.
cards.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers; EU AI Act Art. 25(1)(b)

cards.q: A deployer repurposes a vendor's general office-automation tool to shortlist job applicants — a use the vendor never intended, and one that lands in the high-risk tier. Who now owes the high-risk provider duties?
options: The deployer, because changing the intended purpose so a system becomes high-risk makes it the provider
The vendor, since it built the underlying system
No one, until the vendor updates its documentation
cards.answer: The deployer, because changing the intended purpose so a system becomes high-risk makes it the provider
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the vendor's INTENDED PURPOSE fixed the original classification — whoever changes that purpose so the system becomes high-risk takes the provider role for the new use (Art. 25(1)(c)). (c) would leave a high-risk use ungoverned, which the role-shift rule exists to prevent.
cards.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers; EU AI Act Art. 25(1)(c)

cards.q: Your team fine-tunes a third party's general-purpose model and releases the result under your own brand. Where do you now sit?
options: You take on GPAI provider duties for your modification — documentation, downstream-information and copyright-policy duties attach to you
You remain a mere deployer of the upstream model
The upstream lab remains the only provider, whatever you do
Fine-tuning another lab's model is prohibited without a licence under the AI Act
cards.answer: You take on GPAI provider duties for your modification — documentation, downstream-information and copyright-policy duties attach to you
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): releasing a modified model under your own name is provider activity, not use — the Commission's GPAI guidelines treat significant fine-tunes as making you provider OF THE MODIFICATION, while the upstream lab keeps duties for the base model (contra c). (d) invents an AI Act licensing rule; that question is contract and IP law.
cards.citation: Ch6 §Requirements for General-purpose AI; Commission GPAI guidelines (2025)

cards.q: A deployer's rebuild of a high-risk system has just shifted the provider role onto it. What does the ORIGINAL provider owe under the role-shift rules?
options: Close cooperation: hand over the documentation and technical access the new provider reasonably needs to comply
Nothing — the shift extinguishes every duty it had
It must co-sign the new conformity assessment
cards.answer: Close cooperation: hand over the documentation and technical access the new provider reasonably needs to comply
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): Art. 25(2) keeps the initial provider on the hook for cooperation, information and reasonable technical access. But it does not make it a co-assessor of a system it no longer controls (c) — the conformity duty travels whole to the new provider.
cards.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers; EU AI Act Art. 25(2)

cards.q: Which of these does NOT move provider duties onto a deployer?
options: Rolling the vendor's system out to thousands of staff, used exactly per its instructions and intended purpose
Marketing the system under the deployer's own trademark
Substantially modifying the system while it stays high-risk
Repurposing it so a non-high-risk system becomes high-risk
cards.answer: Rolling the vendor's system out to thousands of staff, used exactly per its instructions and intended purpose
cards.why: Scale of use is not a trigger — the nearest confusable is assuming heavy operational reliance alone converts a deployer. The three statutory triggers are exactly (b), (c) and (d): rebranding, substantial modification, and purpose change into high-risk (Art. 25(1)(a)–(c)).
cards.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers; EU AI Act Art. 25(1)

cards.q: South Korea's AI Framework Act and Japan's AI Promotion Act both took effect recently. Only one imposes enforceable duties on businesses — which, and why?
options: Korea's — it carries high-impact and generative-AI obligations backed by administrative fines; Japan's statute asks businesses only for cooperation efforts, with no penalties
Japan's — it is the older statute and therefore fully enforceable
Both — any statute in force binds companies
Neither — both are purely promotional frameworks
cards.answer: Korea's — it carries high-impact and generative-AI obligations backed by administrative fines; Japan's statute asks businesses only for cooperation efforts, with no penalties
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c): 'binding statute' does not mean 'business duties' — Japan's Act No. 53 of 2025 is binding law addressed to the STATE, with a deliberate no-penalty design, while Korea's Act No. 20676 (in force 2026-01-22) imposes operator duties, softened only by MSIT's 2026 enforcement grace period.
cards.citation: KR AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676, in force 2026-01-22); JP AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025)

cards.q: Same product, two launches: Brussels and London. Structurally, what differs about the AI rules you meet?
options: The EU applies one horizontal statute with risk tiers; the UK routes cross-sector principles through existing regulators, with no AI statute
Both jurisdictions apply comprehensive AI acts of their own
The UK applies the EU AI Act under the withdrawal agreement
The EU has no in-force duties until December 2027, so the launches are equivalent for now
cards.answer: The EU applies one horizontal statute with risk tiers; the UK routes cross-sector principles through existing regulators, with no AI statute
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (c), the retained-EU-law reflex: the AI Act post-dates Brexit and never applied in the UK. (d) fails on currency — the EU's prohibitions, GPAI duties and Article 50 transparency are already live; only the high-risk regime waits until 2027-12-02.
cards.citation: Ch6 §EU AI Act Implementation; AIGP Study Guide §II.C UK pro-innovation approach

cards.q: Texas and Colorado both passed state AI laws. As of August 2026, which one can actually be enforced against you?
options: Texas's TRAIGA — in force since 1 January 2026; Colorado's replacement ADMT law is signed but takes effect 1 January 2027
Colorado's — its landmark AI Act has applied since February 2026
Both are in force
Neither is in force
cards.answer: Texas's TRAIGA — in force since 1 January 2026; Colorado's replacement ADMT law is signed but takes effect 1 January 2027
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205) NEVER took effect — delayed, challenged in court by xAI with DOJ intervening, then repealed and replaced by SB 26-189 (signed 2026-05-14, effective 2027-01-01). Texas's HB 149 has been enforceable by the AG since New Year 2026.

cards.q: Contrast who is bound: the EU AI Act versus the Council of Europe Framework Convention.
options: The AI Act binds operators — providers, deployers, importers — directly; the Convention binds States Parties, reaching companies only through national implementation
Both instruments bind companies directly
Both instruments bind only governments
The Convention binds companies; the AI Act binds member states only
cards.answer: The AI Act binds operators — providers, deployers, importers — directly; the Convention binds States Parties, reaching companies only through national implementation
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (d), the clean inversion: a REGULATION has direct effect on operators across member states, while a TREATY obliges its state parties to act. Mixing up which instrument works which way is the exact error this pairing punishes.
cards.citation: Ch6 §EU AI Act Implementation; CoE Framework Convention CETS 225

cards.q: Two neighbours, two philosophies: how do the EU and Switzerland differ on AI regulation?
options: The EU runs a comprehensive horizontal statute; Switzerland deliberately chose sectoral, technology-neutral law with no AI-specific act — its first bill only reaches consultation by end-2026
Switzerland mirrors the EU AI Act to preserve market access
Both have comprehensive AI statutes; Switzerland's is just newer
Switzerland has banned high-risk AI outright instead of regulating it
cards.answer: The EU runs a comprehensive horizontal statute; Switzerland deliberately chose sectoral, technology-neutral law with no AI-specific act — its first bill only reaches consultation by end-2026
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): 'Brussels effect' logic predicts convergence, but the February 2025 Federal Council decision expressly rejected a horizontal act. The catch for Swiss firms: the EU AI Act still reaches them extraterritorially whenever their systems' output is used in the EU.
cards.citation: Swiss Federal Council AI decision (Feb 2025); Ch6 §Extraterritoriality

cards.q: Canada's generative-AI code, Brazil's PL 2338 and South Korea's framework statute: which one creates enforceable company duties today?
options: South Korea's — its statute is in force; Canada's code is voluntary (AIDA died), and Brazil's bill is still pending
Canada's — the code became binding when AIDA passed
Brazil's — PL 2338 took effect in 2025
All three are binding
cards.answer: South Korea's — its statute is in force; Canada's code is voluntary (AIDA died), and Brazil's bill is still pending
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): AIDA died with Parliament's prorogation and was never revived — Canada's 2023 generative-AI code remains voluntary. (c) fails on status: PL 2338 is still a bill before Brazil's legislature. Korea's Act No. 20676 has been in force since 2026-01-22.
cards.citation: KR AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); Canada GenAI Voluntary Code (2023, AIDA dead); Brazil PL 2338 (pending)

cards.q: Four regimes on your expansion map: EU Article 50 transparency, Korea's AI Framework Act, Texas's TRAIGA, Colorado's SB 26-189. Which is NOT yet imposing duties on 2 August 2026?
options: Colorado's SB 26-189 — signed May 2026 but effective 1 January 2027
EU Article 50 — deferred to December 2027 with the high-risk regime
Korea's AI Framework Act — still in its legislative process
Texas's TRAIGA — enjoined by the courts
cards.answer: Colorado's SB 26-189 — signed May 2026 but effective 1 January 2027
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): the Digital Omnibus deferral hit the ANNEX III high-risk duties, not Article 50, which became enforceable on 2026-08-02. (c) is stale — Korea's Act has been in force since January 2026; (d) borrows the litigation story from COLORADO (xAI/DOJ v. the old SB 24-205) and pins it on the wrong state.
cards.citation: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus); KR Act No. 20676; TRAIGA (HB 149); Colorado SB 26-189

cards.q: Your board wants a recognised credential attesting the company's AI governance system, awarded by an external auditor and usable in every market you enter. What fits?
options: ISO/IEC 42001 — a voluntary, certifiable AI management system standard; certification signals governance maturity but discharges no legal duty
ISO/IEC 42005 — get certified against its impact-assessment checklist
NIST AI RMF certification through a US accreditation body
EU AI Act CE marking, which certifies the whole organisation
cards.answer: ISO/IEC 42001 — a voluntary, certifiable AI management system standard; certification signals governance maturity but discharges no legal duty
cards.why: Nearest confusable is (b): ISO/IEC 42005 is GUIDANCE for AI impact assessments — not a management-system standard and not certifiable. (c) — the NIST AI RMF is voluntary with no certification scheme behind it; (d) — CE marking attests a PRODUCT'S conformity, never an organisation's governance.
cards.citation: AIGP Study Guide §II.D ISO Core AI Standards; ISO/IEC 42001:2023

cards.q: Your board asks which single federal law imposes comprehensive obligations on your AI hiring and lending products across sectors. What do you tell them?
options: None exists — the US regulates AI through existing sectoral statutes and enforcement
The TAKE IT DOWN Act imposes comprehensive cross-sector duties on AI systems
The NIST AI RMF, which binds all companies selling to the government
EO 14179, which directly regulates private-sector AI development
cards.answer: None exists — the US regulates AI through existing sectoral statutes and enforcement
cards.why: The nearest confusable is the TAKE IT DOWN Act — it really is a federal AI statute, but its scope is narrow (non-consensual intimate deepfakes), not comprehensive. The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance, and executive orders bind agencies, not companies.
cards.citation: SG Ch5 §Sectoral and Civil Laws

cards.q: A startup advertises its chatbot as delivering 'fully autonomous legal advice, 99% accurate' with no evidence behind either boast. Which authority reaches this conduct first, and on what theory?
options: The FTC, treating unsubstantiated AI performance claims as deceptive under Section 5
The CFPB, under adverse-action notice rules
No one — marketing claims about AI fall in a gap until Congress passes an AI act
NIST, through mandatory RMF conformity findings
