cards.answer: The FTC, treating unsubstantiated AI performance claims as deceptive under Section 5
cards.why: The nearest confusable is the no-federal-AI-act fallacy: absence of an AI statute is not absence of law — FTC Act §5 already reaches AI-washing. The CFPB's adverse-action rules govern credit decisions, not ad copy, and NIST has no enforcement power at all.
cards.citation: AIGP Body of Knowledge v2.1

cards.q: Your AI credit model turns down an applicant, who asks why. Under US federal credit law, what must your client provide?
options: An adverse-action notice stating the specific principal reasons for the outcome
Nothing, if the model is too complex to explain
A copy of the model documentation and training data
A referral to the FTC's public complaint portal
cards.answer: An adverse-action notice stating the specific principal reasons for the outcome
cards.why: The nearest confusable is the black-box excuse (b): ECOA/Regulation B require specific reasons and the CFPB has said model complexity is no defense. Handing over documentation or routing to the FTC answers a different question — the duty is a reasons notice to the applicant.
cards.citation: ECOA/Reg B; CFPB Circular 2022-03

cards.q: A US customer demands proof that your system 'complies with the NIST AI RMF as required by federal law.' What is wrong with the demand?
options: It is voluntary guidance — no US statute makes conformity with it mandatory
Only FTC-regulated companies must certify against it
It became mandatory for high-risk systems in 2025
Only EU notified bodies can attest against it
cards.answer: It is voluntary guidance — no US statute makes conformity with it mandatory
cards.why: The nearest confusable is ISO/IEC 42001, which IS a certifiable management-system standard — the NIST AI RMF has no certification scheme and no legal mandate. Option (d) imports the EU notified-body machinery, which belongs to AI Act conformity assessment, not NIST.
cards.citation: SG Ch7 §AI Standards and Frameworks

cards.q: Your US counsel maps oversight for three product lines: a credit-underwriting model, a diagnostic-support tool, and a hiring screener. The correct method is to ask:
options: Which existing sector regulator and statute already govern that activity
Whether each product is registered in the federal AI database
Whether the state where the servers sit has ratified the AI treaty
Which NIST profile the vendor selected at design time
cards.answer: Which existing sector regulator and statute already govern that activity
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which imports the EU's high-risk registration database — the US has no such register. The patchwork discipline is activity-based: CFPB/ECOA for credit, FDA for medical devices, EEOC/Title VII for hiring. Framework profiles (d) are voluntary choices, not jurisdictional facts.
cards.citation: SG Ch5 §Sectoral and Civil Laws

cards.q: The FTC sends your company a civil investigative demand about accuracy claims made for your AI screening tool. What is the strongest first response?
options: Produce the evidence you held to substantiate them at the time they were made
Argue the agency lacks jurisdiction because no federal AI statute exists
Point to NIST AI RMF alignment as a complete defense
cards.answer: Produce the evidence you held to substantiate them at the time they were made
cards.why: The nearest confusable is the jurisdiction gambit (b) — Section 5 reaches AI conduct without any AI-specific statute, so that argument loses. Substantiation must pre-date the claim; framework alignment (c) is good hygiene but does not immunize deception.
cards.citation: AIGP Body of Knowledge v2.1

cards.q: A regulator demands an explanation of 4,000 AI-driven credit denials issued last quarter. Your data-science team says the network is not interpretable. What is the compliant position?
options: Notices must give the specific principal reasons — black-box complexity is no excuse
A general statement that the algorithm scored the applicant below threshold satisfies the duty
Reasons are owed only where a human made the final decision
cards.answer: Notices must give the specific principal reasons — black-box complexity is no excuse
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the human-in-the-loop misconception — ECOA's adverse-action duty attaches to the credit decision however it is made. A generic below-threshold line (b) fails the specificity requirement the CFPB reiterated for AI models.
cards.citation: CFPB Circular 2022-03; ECOA/Reg B §1002.9

cards.q: Which statement best captures the US federal posture toward state AI laws in mid-2026?
options: The executive is pushing preemption — a DOJ task force sues states, while Congress has enacted nothing
A federal preemption statute took effect in March 2026
Washington has endorsed the state laws as the model for national legislation
cards.answer: The executive is pushing preemption — a DOJ task force sues states, while Congress has enacted nothing
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the White House sent legislative preemption recommendations to Congress on 2026-03-20, but recommendations are not enacted law. EO 14365 created the DOJ AI Litigation Task Force (established 2026-01-09) to challenge state laws in court — the opposite of endorsement (c).
cards.citation: EO 14365; White House AI legislative recommendations 2026-03-20

cards.q: The one AI-specific law Congress has actually passed does what?
options: Criminalizes non-consensual intimate deepfakes and requires platform notice-and-removal
Imposes risk-tiered duties on high-risk AI systems
Mandates provenance labels on all synthetic media
cards.answer: Criminalizes non-consensual intimate deepfakes and requires platform notice-and-removal
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the EU-style risk-tier model — no US federal statute does that. Provenance labelling (c) is California SB 942's territory, not federal law. The TAKE IT DOWN Act's platform removal process had to be in place by 2026-05-19.
cards.citation: TAKE IT DOWN Act (Pub. L. 119-12)

cards.q: You build AI systems sold into Texas. Under the state's AI governance act, your baseline exposure as a developer centers on what?
options: Prohibited purposes — creating a system with intent to unlawfully discriminate or manipulate behavior is barred
A duty of care with algorithmic impact assessments filed with the attorney general
Mandatory third-party conformity assessment before any sale
Registering each model in a state AI database
cards.answer: Prohibited purposes — creating a system with intent to unlawfully discriminate or manipulate behavior is barred
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — that duty-of-care-plus-impact-assessment design was Colorado's original SB 24-205 model, which TRAIGA deliberately rejected in favor of intent-based prohibitions. Third-party conformity assessment (c) is the EU route; no US state runs one.
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: A plaintiff-side report shows your Texas-deployed screening model produces skewed outcomes by race. Under TRAIGA alone, what determines developer liability?
options: Proof of intent — a discriminatory result by itself does not establish a violation
Whether the outcomes differ at a statistically significant level
Whether the developer completed an annual bias audit
Whether the model appears in the state's high-risk registry
cards.answer: Proof of intent — a discriminatory result by itself does not establish a violation
cards.why: The nearest confusable is Illinois HB 3773, which uses a discriminatory-EFFECT standard — under TRAIGA the same statistics prove nothing without intent. The annual bias audit (c) is New York City's LL144 mechanism, and Texas keeps no high-risk registry (d).
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: Who can bring an action against your company under Texas's AI act, and what happens before any suit?
options: Only the attorney general — after notice and a 60-day cure period
Private plaintiffs, through a statutory private right of action
The state AI council, following a sandbox exit review
Municipal prosecutors in the county of deployment
cards.answer: Only the attorney general — after notice and a 60-day cure period
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the BIPA-style private right of action — TRAIGA expressly has none, which is a large part of why it is 'light-touch'. The sandbox (c) is a testing shelter, not an enforcement gatekeeper.
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: Your firm deploys a persuasion engine inside a Texas consumer app. Which line of the state AI act does compliance review flag first?
options: The prohibition on intentionally manipulating behavior to incite self-harm or criminal conduct
The requirement to file the algorithm with a state registry before launch
The mandatory fundamental-rights impact assessment for deployers
An outright ban on consumer-facing chatbots
cards.answer: The prohibition on intentionally manipulating behavior to incite self-harm or criminal conduct
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — pre-launch algorithm filing is China's mechanism, not Texas's. The fundamental-rights impact assessment (c) is the EU AI Act's deployer duty. TRAIGA reaches deployers through intent-based prohibited uses, not paperwork gates.
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: Two clients ask about the same customer-ranking feature in Texas: a retailer and a city agency. Why do the answers differ?
options: Government bodies face the social-score and biometric-ID bans — private firms face lighter, intent-based rules
Government users are exempt while private firms carry the duties
Both face identical duties under the act
Only federal agencies are covered, so neither client is affected
cards.answer: Government bodies face the social-score and biometric-ID bans — private firms face lighter, intent-based rules
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which inverts the asymmetry: TRAIGA is STRICTER on government (social scoring; capturing biometric identifiers from public data without consent) than on private actors. It is a state law, so (d)'s federal framing is a category error.
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: The Texas attorney general opens an inquiry into your deployed screening tool. Which fact pattern gives you a recognized defense under the act?
options: Substantial adherence to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework
The tool was procured from a reputable vendor
The tool produced no skewed outcomes last quarter
cards.answer: Substantial adherence to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — clean outcome statistics argue effects, but TRAIGA turns on intent and its safe harbors, which include following recognized frameworks like the NIST AI RMF. Vendor reputation (b) is no statutory defense anywhere.
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: A violation notice lands from the Texas attorney general. What does the statute let you do before any enforcement action begins?
options: Cure the cited problem within 60 days
Demand a jury trial in the first instance
Move the matter into the regulatory sandbox retroactively
cards.answer: Cure the cited problem within 60 days
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c): the sandbox is a prospective testing shelter, not an after-the-fact defense. TRAIGA's cure period is the pre-enforcement safety valve — fix it in 60 days and the AG action never starts.
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: Place Texas correctly among US state AI laws as of mid-2026.
options: In force since January 2026 — a cross-sector but light-touch, intent-based comprehensive law
Enacted but postponed to 2027 after a repeal-and-replace
A hiring-only audit ordinance enforced by a city agency
cards.answer: In force since January 2026 — a cross-sector but light-touch, intent-based comprehensive law
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — that is Colorado's trajectory, not Texas's. TRAIGA took effect on schedule (2026-01-01) and is widely described as the third state comprehensive AI law. The hiring-only audit ordinance (c) is NYC Local Law 144.
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: An invitation arrives to enter the Texas regulatory sandbox with a novel biometric product. What does participation actually buy?
options: A supervised testing window with relief from certain state enforcement while conditions are met
Permanent exemption from the state's AI act
Preemption of federal FTC oversight during the trial
cards.answer: A supervised testing window with relief from certain state enforcement while conditions are met
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): sandbox relief is temporary and conditional, never a permanent pass. And no state program can displace federal law (c) — FTC Act §5 still applies inside the sandbox.
cards.citation: Texas Legislature — HB 149 (TRAIGA)

cards.q: From 1 January 2026, an Illinois employer's AI screening tool disadvantages a protected group even though nobody meant it to. What is the legal position?
options: A civil-rights violation — the state's Human Rights Act now reaches AI with discriminatory effect, no intent required
Lawful unless plaintiffs prove an intent to discriminate
Governed only by the federal EEOC, not state law
Permitted if the vendor certified the tool as bias-free
cards.answer: A civil-rights violation — the state's Human Rights Act now reaches AI with discriminatory effect, no intent required
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — that intent-based standard is Texas TRAIGA's, and HB 3773 pointedly chose the opposite: effect suffices. Vendor certification (d) shifts nothing; the duty sits on the employer under the amended IHRA.
cards.citation: Illinois General Assembly — HB 3773 (P.A. 103-0804)

cards.q: Your client wants to roll out fingerprint time-clocks across Illinois warehouses. Before any scanning starts, the state's biometric statute requires what?
options: Written notice and a written release from each worker, plus a public retention schedule
A bias audit published on the company website
Registration of the fingerprint templates with the state
Nothing, provided the data never leaves company premises
cards.answer: Written notice and a written release from each worker, plus a public retention schedule
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the published bias audit is NYC LL144's hiring rule, a different instrument and city. BIPA §15 demands informed written consent and a retention/destruction policy before collection; on-premises storage (d) is no exemption.
cards.citation: 740 ILCS 14 (BIPA)

cards.q: An Illinois recruiter's model never sees race but heavily weights applicants' home postal areas. Under the 2026 employment-AI amendment, that practice is:
options: Expressly restricted — ZIP code may not be used as a proxy for protected classes
Lawful, because location is not a protected characteristic
A biometric-privacy violation
Actionable only under federal redlining rules
cards.answer: Expressly restricted — ZIP code may not be used as a proxy for protected classes
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — BIPA is the other famous Illinois statute, but it covers biometric identifiers, not geographic proxies. HB 3773 names ZIP-code-as-proxy explicitly, so no resort to federal redlining doctrine (d) is needed.
cards.citation: Illinois General Assembly — HB 3773 (P.A. 103-0804)

cards.q: An employee charge says your client used AI in promotion decisions without telling anyone. Even if the tool turns out to be fair, what exposure remains?
options: Failing to notify workers of AI use is itself a violation of the amended Human Rights Act
None — notice matters only where discrimination is proven
Only contract damages owed to the software vendor
cards.answer: Failing to notify workers of AI use is itself a violation of the amended Human Rights Act
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): HB 3773 makes the notice duty freestanding — a silent deployment violates the act even absent any discriminatory outcome. The vendor relationship (c) is irrelevant to the civil-rights charge.
cards.citation: Illinois General Assembly — HB 3773 (P.A. 103-0804)

cards.q: A demand letter arrives on behalf of thousands of workers over years of un-consented voiceprint collection in Illinois. What makes this statute uniquely dangerous to defendants?
options: A private right of action with statutory damages per violation, no proof of actual harm needed
Criminal liability for company executives
Automatic revocation of the company's business license
cards.answer: A private right of action with statutory damages per violation, no proof of actual harm needed
cards.why: The nearest confusable is HB 3773's route — employment-AI charges there go through the IDHR administrative process, whereas BIPA lets plaintiffs sue directly for statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent and $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation, with no proof of actual harm required (Rosenbach v. Six Flags) — multiplied across a class of thousands of workers. Neither criminal liability (b) nor license loss (c) is BIPA's mechanism.
cards.citation: 740 ILCS 14 (BIPA)

cards.q: What is the mid-2026 status of Illinois's implementing rules for the employment-AI amendment?
options: Proposed in May 2026, withdrawn in June — the statute applies without final regulations
Final since January 2026, alongside the statute
The statute is suspended until the rules issue
cards.answer: Proposed in May 2026, withdrawn in June — the statute applies without final regulations
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the suspension myth: statutory duties operate regardless of the rulemaking's fate. IDHR proposed Subpart J on 2026-05-15, then temporarily withdrew it on 2026-06-02 to coordinate with other agencies — no adopted rules exist, but HB 3773 binds anyway.
cards.citation: IDHR proposed Subpart J rules, withdrawn 2026-06-02

cards.q: Before your client screens New York City candidates with an automated employment decision tool, the local law's threshold requirement is:
options: An independent bias audit completed within the past year
A conformity assessment and CE marking
Filing the algorithm with the city's consumer-affairs agency
Written consent from every candidate
cards.answer: An independent bias audit completed within the past year
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d): LL144 requires candidate NOTICE, not consent — consent-before-collection is Illinois BIPA's model. CE marking (b) belongs to the EU regime, and there is no algorithm filing in NYC (c); that pattern is China's.
cards.citation: NYC DCWP — Automated Employment Decision Tools (Local Law 144)

cards.q: The bias audit for your client's hiring tool is complete. What must happen to the results?
options: A summary must be posted publicly on the employer's website
They are filed confidentially with the enforcement agency
They go only to affected candidates on request
They must be notarized and retained internally for five years
cards.answer: A summary must be posted publicly on the employer's website
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — confidential regulator filing is how China's algorithm-filing regime works, but LL144 chose sunlight: the summary is public. On-request or internal-only handling (c, d) both fail the publication duty.
cards.citation: NYC DCWP — Automated Employment Decision Tools (Local Law 144)

cards.q: How far in advance must a New York City employer tell candidates an automated tool will assess them?
options: Ten business days before use
At the moment the application is submitted
Within thirty days after the decision issues
Never, provided the audit summary is published
cards.answer: Ten business days before use
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — notice AFTER the decision is the ECOA adverse-action pattern from credit law; LL144's notice is prospective. Publication of the audit (d) is a separate, parallel duty and does not substitute for individual notice.
cards.citation: NYC DCWP — Automated Employment Decision Tools (Local Law 144)

cards.q: Enforcement of the city's hiring-tool rule began 5 July 2023. Which actor does it actually bind?
options: Employers and employment agencies using the tool — not the vendor that built it
The software vendor, as the system's provider
Vendor and employer jointly and severally
The independent auditors who review the tool
cards.answer: Employers and employment agencies using the tool — not the vendor that built it
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the EU-style provider framing — LL144 places no duty on developers or vendors at all; the deployer-side employer carries everything. Auditors (d) are third-party service providers, not duty-bearers.
cards.citation: NYC DCWP — Automated Employment Decision Tools (Local Law 144)

cards.q: The city's consumer-affairs department alleges your client ran an unaudited screening tool for three months. How does the exposure accumulate?
options: Per violation per day — each day of use is a separate violation, $500 to $1,500
One flat fine per non-compliant tool
Exposure begins only on a second offense
cards.answer: Per violation per day — each day of use is a separate violation, $500 to $1,500
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): LL144 penalties are not a one-off — each day the tool runs without a current audit is a fresh violation, so three months compounds fast. There is no first-offense grace (c); enforcement has run since 2023-07-05.
cards.citation: NYC DCWP — Automated Employment Decision Tools (Local Law 144)

cards.q: To answer a city inquiry, your client offers a review of its hiring tool that the vendor ran itself two years ago. Name the two defects.
options: It is not independent, and it is older than the one-year currency window
It was not notarized and not filed with the state
Only the vendor's own review is acceptable, so the age is the sole problem
cards.answer: It is not independent, and it is older than the one-year currency window
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), which inverts the independence rule — the auditor must NOT be someone involved in developing or using the tool, so a vendor self-review fails per se. LL144 has no notarization or state-filing mechanics (b).
cards.citation: NYC DCWP — Automated Employment Decision Tools (Local Law 144)

cards.q: A December 2025 state review examined how the city polices its hiring-tool rule. What did it find, and what should compliance teams infer for 2026?
options: Enforcement was called ineffective; the agency accepted the recommendations, so scrutiny is expected to tighten
The rule was found unconstitutional and struck down
It found near-universal employer compliance, so risk is falling
cards.answer: Enforcement was called ineffective; the agency accepted the recommendations, so scrutiny is expected to tighten
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — no court touched LL144; this was the NYS Comptroller's performance audit of DCWP (2025-12-02). Weak past enforcement plus accepted recommendations signals MORE enforcement ahead, the opposite of (c)'s complacency read.
cards.citation: NYS Comptroller — LL144 enforcement audit 2025-12-02

cards.q: Your client conflates the city hiring rule with New York State's new AI law signed in December 2025. Set them straight.
options: The state law targets frontier-model safety — a separate regime that leaves the city ordinance untouched
The state law replaced the city ordinance on signing
They are the same statute at different procedural stages
cards.answer: The state law targets frontier-model safety — a separate regime that leaves the city ordinance untouched
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the preemption assumption — the RAISE Act (signed 2025-12-19) regulates frontier-model developers at state level and does not displace LL144's employer-side hiring duties. Different duty-bearers, different subject matter.
cards.citation: NY RAISE Act (signed 2025-12-19)

cards.q: Your client runs a generative service with two million monthly California visitors. As of today, 2 August 2026, the state's AI transparency act requires it to offer:
options: A free public AI-detection tool plus manifest and latent disclosures in AI-generated content
Publication of a high-level training-data summary
An annual independent bias audit with a posted summary
Age verification before any content generation
cards.answer: A free public AI-detection tool plus manifest and latent disclosures in AI-generated content
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the training-data summary is AB 2013's separate duty, not SB 942's. SB 942 became operative today (2026-08-02, after the AB 853 delay) for covered providers over one million monthly visitors or users; the bias audit (c) is NYC's mechanism.
cards.citation: California SB 942 (as amended by AB 853, 2025-10-13)

cards.q: Compliance was planned around a 1 January 2026 start for California's provenance law. What actually happened to that date?
options: An amendment moved the operative date to 2 August 2026, with large-platform duties following in 2027
The law was repealed and replaced with a narrower one
It took effect on schedule at the start of the year
A court enjoined it indefinitely
cards.answer: An amendment moved the operative date to 2 August 2026, with large-platform duties following in 2027
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — repeal-and-replace is Colorado's story; California merely DELAYED via AB 853 (chaptered 2025-10-13). No court has enjoined SB 942 (d). The lesson is date-churn: track amendments, not just enactments.
cards.citation: California SB 942 (as amended by AB 853, 2025-10-13)

cards.q: Since January 2026, what must a generative-AI developer publish about the data behind any system offered to Californians?
options: High-level documentation of the datasets used to train the system
The full training corpus, on request from any user
Nothing, unless the system is classed high-risk
Only records of data purchased from third parties
cards.answer: High-level documentation of the datasets used to train the system
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which overreads AB 2013 — the duty is a high-level summary (sources, types, copyright/personal-data flags), never corpus disclosure. Option (c) imports EU risk-tier gating; AB 2013 applies without any risk classification.
cards.citation: California AB 2013 (eff. 2026-01-01)

cards.q: A Californian asks to opt out of your client's automated tool that decides loan approvals. Which regime governs, and what does it grant?
options: The CCPA ADMT regulations — notice, opt-out and access rights around significant decisions
The AI transparency act's detection-tool duties
The civil-rights agency's employment rules
A federal ADMT preemption framework
cards.answer: The CCPA ADMT regulations — notice, opt-out and access rights around significant decisions
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — the CRD's FEHA rules also reach automated decisions but only in EMPLOYMENT; lending is a 'significant decision' under the CPPA's ADMT regulations. No federal ADMT framework exists (d), and SB 942 (b) is about content provenance, not decisions.
cards.citation: CPPA — Final ADMT regulations (eff. 2026-01-01)

cards.q: Your client's sales chatbot converses with California consumers without ever saying it is software. Where is the exposure?
options: The bot-disclosure law — bots used to sell must clearly reveal they are not human
The provenance act's latent-disclosure duties
Nowhere; conversational identity is unregulated in the state
The intent-based manipulation ban in the state AI act
cards.answer: The bot-disclosure law — bots used to sell must clearly reveal they are not human
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): SB 942 marks AI-GENERATED CONTENT, while SB 1001 governs conversational identity when a bot incentivizes a sale or influences a vote — different disclosure objects. Option (d) describes Texas TRAIGA, the wrong state.
cards.citation: California SB 1001 (B.O.T. Act)

cards.q: An employer uses an algorithmic ranking system for California hires. Since October 2025, which body's rules directly govern discrimination risk from that system?
options: The Civil Rights Department's FEHA automated-decision employment rules
The privacy agency's ADMT regulations alone
New York City's consumer-affairs department
None — California employment AI awaits a 2027 statute
cards.answer: The Civil Rights Department's FEHA automated-decision employment rules
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the CPPA's ADMT regs also touch employment decisions, but the DISCRIMINATION question runs through the CRD's FEHA rules (effective 2025-10-01). Option (d) is false: those rules are already in force, no waiting period.
cards.citation: CRD — FEHA automated-decision regulations (eff. 2025-10-01)

cards.q: A wave of opt-out and access requests hits your client's decisioning tool after a viral privacy post. Counsel asks what the timeline actually demands. Your answer:
options: Build the opt-out and access machinery now — the rules took effect in 2026, with significant-decision compliance due by 1 January 2027
Ignore them; nothing is in force until 2028
Honor them only for fully autonomous decisions with no human involvement
cards.answer: Build the opt-out and access machinery now — the rules took effect in 2026, with significant-decision compliance due by 1 January 2027
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which misreads the phase-in as total deferral — the CPPA regulations have been effective since 2026-01-01; only the significant-decision ADMT compliance deadline runs to 2027-01-01. Option (c) invents an autonomy threshold the rules do not use.
cards.citation: CPPA — Final ADMT regulations (eff. 2026-01-01)

cards.q: Your client develops frontier models. One behaves in a way that creates a critical safety event. Under California law, who must hear about it?
options: The state Office of Emergency Services, under the frontier-AI transparency act's incident-reporting duty
The city consumer-affairs department
The EU AI Office, under serious-incident rules
cards.answer: The state Office of Emergency Services, under the frontier-AI transparency act's incident-reporting duty
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — the EU AI Act's serious-incident reporting is the parallel mechanism but the wrong jurisdiction; SB 53 routes critical incidents to California's OES. The city consumer-affairs channel (b) is NYC LL144's enforcement home, unrelated to frontier models.
cards.citation: California SB 53 — Transparency in Frontier AI Act

cards.q: Beyond incident reports, what does California's frontier-AI law demand of the largest developers, on pain of penalties up to $1M?
options: A published safety framework and whistleblower protections
CE marking of each model before release
Divestiture of compute above a licensing threshold
cards.answer: A published safety framework and whistleblower protections
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — CE marking is EU conformity iconography with no California analogue. SB 53 is a transparency statute: publish the safety framework, protect whistleblowers, report critical incidents. It licenses nothing and divests nothing (c).
cards.citation: California SB 53 — Transparency in Frontier AI Act

cards.q: Summarize how California allocates AI duties across the actors in a supply chain.
options: Statute by statute — training-data duties on developers, provenance on large generative providers, ADMT rights against businesses deploying the tools
Through a single provider-deployer-importer scheme like the EU's
By consolidating every duty on whoever deploys the system
cards.answer: Statute by statute — training-data duties on developers, provenance on large generative providers, ADMT rights against businesses deploying the tools
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): unlike the EU AI Act's single role taxonomy, California has no unified scheme — AB 2013 names developers, SB 942 covered providers, the CCPA regs businesses. Option (c) describes Colorado's deployer-weighted replacement law, not California.
cards.citation: California AB 2013; SB 942; CPPA ADMT regulations

cards.q: A colleague budgets 2026 compliance work for Colorado's landmark duty-of-care AI law. Correct the record.
options: It never took effect — repealed and replaced in May 2026 before its delayed start date arrived
It has applied since February 2026 as originally scheduled
It applies, but only to government agencies
It survived judicial review and has applied since June 2026
cards.answer: It never took effect — repealed and replaced in May 2026 before its delayed start date arrived
cards.why: The nearest confusables are (b) and (d), which recite the two effective dates that never arrived: 2026-02-01 was pushed to 2026-06-30 by SB 25B-004, and the repeal-and-replace (2026-05-14) landed first. SB 24-205 produced zero days of operative law.
cards.citation: Colorado General Assembly — SB26-189; SB 25B-004

cards.q: What replaced Colorado's original AI act, and when does it start to bite?
options: A narrower ADMT disclosure law, signed May 2026, effective 1 January 2027
A comprehensive intent-based act effective January 2026
Nothing — the field was deregulated by design
A ballot measure that took effect immediately on passage
cards.answer: A narrower ADMT disclosure law, signed May 2026, effective 1 January 2027
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which describes TEXAS's TRAIGA — in force since January 2026 and intent-based. Colorado's SB 26-189 is a disclosure/transparency regime for automated decision technology and does not operate until 2027-01-01.
cards.citation: Colorado General Assembly — SB26-189

cards.q: Under Colorado's replacement law, which actor carries most of the load once it operates?
options: Those deploying automated decision technology — disclosure duties sit mainly with them
Developers, through a duty of care and impact assessments
Importers and distributors of AI systems
Auditors certified by the attorney general
cards.answer: Those deploying automated decision technology — disclosure duties sit mainly with them
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the developer duty-of-care with impact assessments was the REPEALED SB 24-205 design; SB 26-189 largely eliminated the developer/deployer duty split and weighted what remains toward deployers. Importers (c) are an EU role with no Colorado analogue.
cards.citation: Colorado General Assembly — SB26-189

cards.q: List the Colorado sequence a compliance calendar had to track between 2024 and 2026.
options: Enacted 2024 → start date delayed → enforcement stayed amid litigation → repealed and replaced, new date 2027
Enacted 2024 → effective 2025 → amended 2026
Proposed 2024 → died in committee → reintroduced 2026
Enacted 2024 → preempted by a federal statute in 2026
cards.answer: Enacted 2024 → start date delayed → enforcement stayed amid litigation → repealed and replaced, new date 2027
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d) — the DOJ did intervene in the court challenge, but no federal preemption statute exists; the reversal was Colorado's own legislature. Four moves in two years is the date-churn lesson: a compliance date is not a fact you memorise once.
cards.citation: Colorado General Assembly — SB26-189; SB 25B-004

cards.q: What role did the courts play in Colorado's AI-law reversal?
options: An AI company sued the attorney general, the DOJ intervened, and enforcement was stayed weeks before the repeal
The state supreme court struck the law down as unconstitutional
None — the repeal was purely a legislative initiative with no litigation backdrop
cards.answer: An AI company sued the attorney general, the DOJ intervened, and enforcement was stayed weeks before the repeal
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): no court ever ruled the law unconstitutional — xAI's suit (filed 2026-04-09, DOJ intervening) produced a stay, and the LEGISLATURE then repealed and replaced it. Option (c) erases the litigation pressure that shaped the outcome.
cards.citation: Colorado General Assembly — SB26-189; xAI v. Colorado AG (2026)

cards.q: Name the pieces of the original Colorado model that the 2026 replacement dropped.
options: Duty of care, risk-management programs, impact assessments and attorney-general reporting
All disclosure and transparency duties
Only the definition of algorithmic discrimination
cards.answer: Duty of care, risk-management programs, impact assessments and attorney-general reporting
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which inverts the outcome — disclosure and transparency are exactly what SB 26-189 KEPT; the heavyweight governance machinery is what went. That deletion is why commentators describe the replacement as substantially narrower.
cards.citation: Colorado General Assembly — SB26-189

cards.q: It is 2 August 2026 and your client operates decisioning tools in Colorado. Which AI-specific state obligations bind today?
options: None yet — the replacement law starts 1 January 2027, and its predecessor never operated
The original act's duty of care, pending the repeal taking effect
The replacement law's disclosure duties, in force since signing
cards.answer: None yet — the replacement law starts 1 January 2027, and its predecessor never operated
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the signing-date-equals-effective-date error — SB 26-189 was signed 2026-05-14 but operates from 2027-01-01. Option (b) treats a dead law as live. Colorado today is a gap: general consumer and privacy law apply, nothing AI-specific.
cards.citation: Colorado General Assembly — SB26-189

cards.q: A prospect insists Canada's federal AI bill will govern your deployment next year. What actually happened to that bill?
options: It died on the order paper at the January 2025 prorogation and was never revived
It passed and takes effect in 2027
It is in committee before final reading
It was folded into the federal privacy statute
cards.answer: It died on the order paper at the January 2025 prorogation and was never revived
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the still-in-committee myth — AIDA (Bill C-27 Part 3) is dead, not dormant, and no successor bill has been tabled as of August 2026. The government has said future AI legislation will proceed separately from privacy reform, so (d) is backwards too.
cards.citation: ISED — AIDA (Bill C-27) companion document; prorogation 2025-01-06

cards.q: With no binding statute for the private sector, what actually anchors AI governance expectations for Canadian industry?
options: The 2023 voluntary code of conduct for advanced generative systems, joined by signatories
The Directive on Automated Decision-Making
A dedicated AI chapter inside PIPEDA
Provincial AI acts in Ontario and Quebec
cards.answer: The 2023 voluntary code of conduct for advanced generative systems, joined by signatories
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the ADM Directive is genuinely binding, but only on the federal government's own decision systems, so it sets no private-sector expectations. PIPEDA has no AI chapter (c), and no province has a general private-sector AI act (d) — Ontario's 2024 act reaches only public-sector use.
cards.citation: Voluntary Code of Conduct on Advanced Generative AI (2023)

cards.q: Canada does have one binding AI instrument. Who must obey it?
options: Federal institutions using automated decision systems for their own administrative decisions
Any company doing business in Canada above a revenue threshold
Signatories of the generative-AI code of conduct
cards.answer: Federal institutions using automated decision systems for their own administrative decisions
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — code signatories make voluntary commitments, which is the opposite of binding law. The ADM Directive binds government deployers only; a federally REGULATED private company (banks, airlines) is still outside its scope, which trips up option (b) thinkers.
cards.citation: Directive on Automated Decision-Making

cards.q: What did June 2026 bring for Canadian AI policy, and did it create any duties?
options: A national strategy with a $1B compute fund — it signals future legislation but imposes nothing
A binding AI safety statute with immediate effect
Accession to the EU AI Act's third-country mechanism
cards.answer: A national strategy with a $1B compute fund — it signals future legislation but imposes nothing
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the 'AI for All' strategy (launched 2026-06-04) and the February 2026 consultation summary signal rules on safety testing and oversight to come, but nothing has been tabled. Option (c) is a category error — the EU AI Act has no accession mechanism for states.
cards.citation: Canada.ca — National AI Strategy launch (2026-06-04)

cards.q: Ottawa insiders say the dead federal AI bill is coming back, and clients ask whether to stand up a compliance program now. Your call?
options: No binding duties exist or are tabled — track developments rather than build to a ghost statute
Begin conformity assessments now to get ahead of enactment
Adopt the EU AI Act wholesale as a proxy for the coming Canadian law
cards.answer: No binding duties exist or are tabled — track developments rather than build to a ghost statute
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the comply-now trap: AIDA died at the January 2025 prorogation and no successor text exists to comply WITH — building conformity machinery against a rumour misallocates capital. Voluntarily adopting good practice differs from (c)'s pretence that EU law maps onto a nonexistent Canadian statute.
cards.citation: ISED — AIDA (Bill C-27) companion document; prorogation 2025-01-06

cards.q: Where does Brazil's risk-based AI bill stand as of August 2026?
options: Approved by the Senate in December 2024, still before a special committee of the Chamber of Deputies — not law
In force since January 2026
Vetoed by the president after passage
Withdrawn by its sponsors pending redrafting
cards.answer: Approved by the Senate in December 2024, still before a special committee of the Chamber of Deputies — not law
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the Latin American framework actually in force since January 2026 is PERU's, not Brazil's. PL 2338/2023 passed the Senate on 2024-12-10 and sits 'Aguardando Parecer' in the Chamber; there has been no floor vote, veto or withdrawal.
cards.citation: Câmara dos Deputados — PL 2338/2023 tramitação

cards.q: Your contracts team wants to allocate 'developer', 'distributor' and 'applier' obligations for a Brazilian rollout, copying the AI bill's own language. What is the problem?
options: Those graded role duties bind no one yet — the bill is not enacted
The bill actually uses the EU's provider-deployer-importer labels
Distributors were struck from the Senate text
The duties already apply through data-authority regulation
cards.answer: Those graded role duties bind no one yet — the bill is not enacted
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d) — the ANPD is tipped to coordinate the bill's future enforcement system, but it has issued no binding AI-role duties; contracting as if the bill were law imports obligations that do not exist. The role names themselves are correctly Brazilian (b is wrong): the bill does not copy EU labels.
cards.citation: Câmara dos Deputados — PL 2338/2023 tramitação

cards.q: Meanwhile, what actually governs an AI system processing Brazilians' personal data today?
options: The LGPD — the general data-protection law, including its review right over automated decisions
The AI bill's high-risk chapter, applied provisionally
The EU AI Act, extraterritorially
Nothing, until the AI bill passes
cards.answer: The LGPD — the general data-protection law, including its review right over automated decisions
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d), the legal-vacuum myth — no AI act does not mean no law; the LGPD's Article 20 already gives review rights over automated decisions. Provisional application (b) is not a thing in Brazilian legislative procedure, and the EU AI Act (c) reaches EU-market conduct, not domestic Brazilian processing.

cards.q: If Brazil's bill passes as drafted, how would enforcement be organized?
options: A national AI governance system (SIA) coordinated by the data-protection authority, the ANPD
A new standalone AI agency replacing the data-protection authority
State-level consumer bodies acting independently
cards.answer: A national AI governance system (SIA) coordinated by the data-protection authority, the ANPD
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the design builds on the EXISTING authority rather than replacing it: the ANPD is tipped as coordinator of the SIA, with sector regulators retained. Fragmented state-level enforcement (c) is the US pattern, not the bill's.
cards.citation: Câmara dos Deputados — PL 2338/2023 tramitação

cards.q: A May 2026 date was set for the Chamber floor vote on Brazil's AI bill. What happened, and what is the sticking point?
options: The vote slipped without being held — copyright remuneration remains the main fight
It passed narrowly and awaits Senate concurrence
It failed on the floor and the bill was archived
cards.answer: The vote slipped without being held — copyright remuneration remains the main fight
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the Senate already approved the bill in 2024; the pending step is the Chamber, and the scheduled 27 May 2026 vote simply never happened. Archiving (c) would require a floor defeat that never occurred; the bill remains live in committee.
cards.citation: Câmara dos Deputados — PL 2338/2023 tramitação

cards.q: Headline: 'Brazilian AI Act imminent.' A client asks whether to stand up an EU-style conformity program for Brazil this quarter. Best advice?
options: Not yet — track the bill; today's binding work is LGPD compliance
Yes — the duties will apply retroactively once enacted
Yes — the Senate vote already made the bill binding
cards.answer: Not yet — track the bill; today's binding work is LGPD compliance
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), which mistakes bicameral progress for enactment — Senate approval in 2024 created no duties; the Chamber has not voted. Retroactive application (b) is not how the bill is drafted. Budget goes to the LGPD obligations that bind now.
cards.citation: Câmara dos Deputados — PL 2338/2023 tramitação; LGPD

cards.q: Which Latin American jurisdiction has a binding general AI framework actually in force, and since when?
options: Peru — its AI law's implementing regulation took effect in January 2026
Brazil — since the Senate vote of December 2024
Chile — under a 2025 AI statute
None; the region remains voluntary-only
cards.answer: Peru — its AI law's implementing regulation took effect in January 2026
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the Senate-vote-as-law error — Brazil's PL 2338 is still pending in the Chamber. Peru's Law 31814 (2023) gained operative force through Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM on 2026-01-22, making it the first binding general AI framework in the region.

cards.q: Your product team asks how Peru's framework sorts AI uses. The structure is:
options: Risk tiers, including prohibited uses and a high-risk band carrying heavier duties
A single horizontal duty set applying equally to every system
Sector-by-sector rules issued by each ministry
Voluntary self-classification by the operator
cards.answer: Risk tiers, including prohibited uses and a high-risk band carrying heavier duties
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — sector-by-sector regulation is the US pattern; Peru's reglamento is a general framework with EU-flavoured tiering (prohibited and high-risk categories). Classification is legal, not self-selected (d).

cards.q: Compared with the EU AI Act, Peru's regime is best characterized as:
options: Promotion-oriented and lighter-touch — an innovation-promoting law with risk safeguards attached
Stricter, with criminal penalties for high-risk misuse
A verbatim transposition of the EU text
Purely aspirational, with no binding force
cards.answer: Promotion-oriented and lighter-touch — an innovation-promoting law with risk safeguards attached
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d), which understates it — the reglamento's duties are binding; 'promotion-oriented' describes the statute's purpose (economic and social development), not an absence of force. Option (c) overstates the EU likeness: the tiering rhymes, the weight does not.

cards.q: Peru's regulation distinguishes actor categories. Which pairing does it use, and who bears more?
options: Developers and implementers — with duties weighted toward those deploying high-risk uses
Providers and importers, per the EU taxonomy
Operators split into development and utilization classes
Platforms and end users, with duties on platforms
cards.answer: Developers and implementers — with duties weighted toward those deploying high-risk uses
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c) — the development/utilization operator split is SOUTH KOREA's taxonomy, not Peru's. Option (b) borrows EU labels the decree does not use. The reglamento reaches developers and implementers/deployers, with the weight on high-risk deployment.

cards.q: Peru's digital-government secretariat questions your client's high-risk deployment. Which duty cluster must the response evidence?
options: Transparency, security and audit obligations under the reglamento's high-risk band
CE marking and an EU declaration of conformity
A published bias-audit summary per the municipal hiring rule
cards.answer: Transparency, security and audit obligations under the reglamento's high-risk band
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — CE marking and declarations of conformity are EU AI Act artifacts with no Peruvian counterpart. The published bias-audit summary (c) is NYC LL144's employer duty. Peru's decree asks for transparency, security and auditability evidence.

cards.q: Your client argues nothing in Peru applied before 2026, so early-2025 conduct is beyond reach. Why is that not quite right?
options: Several provisions took effect the day after the decree's September 2025 publication; the rest followed in January 2026
The whole framework has applied since the 2023 law passed
Nothing applies until 2027 under the phase-in schedule
cards.answer: Several provisions took effect the day after the decree's September 2025 publication; the rest followed in January 2026
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — Law 31814 (2023) was principles-level; operative duties arrived only with the reglamento, so dating everything to 2023 overreaches just as (c)'s 2027 deferral underreaches. The decree published 2025-09-09 with a phased entry ending 2026-01-22.

cards.q: Which body sits at the center of Peru's AI governance architecture?
options: The Presidency of the Council of Ministers, through its digital transformation secretariat
An independent AI commission modeled on the EU AI Office
The central bank's financial-technology unit
cards.answer: The Presidency of the Council of Ministers, through its digital transformation secretariat
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — Peru created no standalone AI office; oversight runs through the existing PCM/SGTD machinery inside the National Digital Transformation System. The central-bank framing (c) would make the regime sectoral, which it is not.

cards.q: Peru's reglamento was published on 9 September 2025 yet is dated in force from 22 January 2026. What explains the gap?
options: The decree set a vacatio legis of 90 business days from publication — the general framework applied once that period expired
The government postponed it by emergency decree after industry pushback
It awaited congressional ratification before it could take effect
cards.answer: The decree set a vacatio legis of 90 business days from publication — the general framework applied once that period expired
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — no postponement ever happened; the interval was designed in from day one, and it is counted in BUSINESS days, not calendar days, which is why it stretches from September into late January. (c) misreads the instrument: a supreme decree regulating Law 31814 needs no congressional ratification.

cards.q: Your Seoul lab builds a credit-scoring model that MSIT's criteria class as high-impact AI. As the developing business, what does the Framework Act require of you before and during service?
options: Establish a risk-management plan and ensure explainability, human oversight, user protection and documentation
Complete a third-party conformity assessment and affix a national certification mark
Publish an annual transparency report; substantive duties fall on the end user
Nothing yet — high-impact duties do not take effect until 2027
cards.answer: Establish a risk-management plan and ensure explainability, human oversight, user protection and documentation
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): a conformity-assessment-plus-marking route is the EU AI Act's machinery — Korea's Act imposes direct statutory duties on the operator with no CE-style marking. (d) transplants the EU's deferred Annex III timeline (December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus); Korea's Act has been fully in force since 2026-01-22. Note the taxonomy: an 'AI development business operator' sits roughly where the EU's provider does, but Korea's Act uses the operator terms, not the EU ones.
cards.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); CSET official-text translation

cards.q: Your generative model produces both photorealistic video of real people and obviously stylised cartoon output for the Korean market. How does the Framework Act treat the two output streams differently?
options: Realistic synthetic output needs a visible label; clearly artificial output may carry machine-readable watermarks instead
Both streams need visible on-screen labels — no machine-readable alternative exists
Neither needs marking; Korea only requires advance notice that generative AI is in use
Only output re-shared by platforms must be marked, and the platform bears the duty
cards.answer: Realistic synthetic output needs a visible label; clearly artificial output may carry machine-readable watermarks instead
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d): a platform-side verify-and-relabel duty is China's regime under the Labelling Measures and GB 45438-2025 — in Korea the duty stays with the operator. (c) confuses the separate advance-notice duty with output marking: both exist, and notice does not substitute for marking realistic content.
cards.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); FPF — South Korea's New AI Framework Act

cards.q: Your foundation model's training run exceeds the compute threshold set under Korea's Enforcement Decree. What extra obligation attaches to your business?
options: Safety obligations for large-scale AI, including reporting the risk assessment to MSIT
Notify the Personal Information Protection Commission and pause deployment
Register the model in a public algorithm registry before launch
Obtain an operating licence from a national AI safety institute
cards.answer: Safety obligations for large-scale AI, including reporting the risk assessment to MSIT
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c): registry filing is China's mechanism under its algorithm provisions — Korea's compute-threshold trigger is a safety-assurance-and-report duty owed to MSIT, the AI ministry. (b) points at the privacy regulator, which owns personal-data questions, not large-scale-AI safety; no licensing regime exists.
cards.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); CSET official-text translation

cards.q: A Busan bank licenses a third-party screening model and runs it on loan applicants under its own authority. Under the Framework Act, which duties land on the bank?
options: Safety and reliability measures plus user-protection duties, as the AI utilization business operator using the system
None — the Act binds only the business that developed the model
EU-style deployer duties, imported by reference into Korean law
Only a duty to appoint a domestic representative
cards.answer: Safety and reliability measures plus user-protection duties, as the AI utilization business operator using the system
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c): Korea's Act attaches its own duty content to the bank's use — safety/reliability measures and protection of the users the model is run on — rather than importing the EU's deployer duty set; the utilization operator sits roughly where the EU deployer does, but the duties come from the Korean statute alone. (d) is the foreign-operator threshold duty, irrelevant to a domestic bank.
cards.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); FPF — South Korea's New AI Framework Act

cards.q: Your US company serves Korean users at scale with no establishment in Korea. What does the Framework Act add once you cross the qualifying thresholds?
options: Appoint a domestic representative in Korea
Route the product through a locally established importer that takes over your obligations
Nothing — the Act has no reach over foreign operators
Move all Korean user data onshore before continuing service
cards.answer: Appoint a domestic representative in Korea
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): an importer that assumes responsibility for a third-country product is an EU AI Act role — Korea has no importer category; the Act reaches foreign operators affecting the Korean market directly and adds a local-representative duty above thresholds. (c) is wrong because extraterritorial application is explicit. Unlike the EU's authorised-representative duty (Art. 22), which is role-based and attaches to every third-country provider of a high-risk system regardless of scale, Korea's duty is threshold-triggered — it keys on user/revenue scale.
cards.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); Cooley — South Korea's AI Basic Act

cards.q: Your customer-service product answers Korean consumers using a generative model. What must users receive before they interact with it?
options: Advance notification that generative AI is being used
A copy of the operator's risk-management plan
An opt-out that routes them to a human by default
Nothing, unless MSIT has designated the generative service high-impact
cards.answer: Advance notification that generative AI is being used
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d): the generative-AI transparency duty is a standalone obligation that applies regardless of high-impact designation — the two tiers trigger different duty sets. (b) confuses user-facing transparency with the high-impact operator's internal documentation, which is never handed to consumers.
cards.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); CSET official-text translation

cards.q: MSIT writes asking you to evidence whether your foreign-run service crossed the thresholds that trigger the local-representative duty. What actually decides it?
options: User numbers and revenue measured against the Enforcement Decree criteria
Training compute measured against the large-scale-AI threshold
Whether the service has been designated high-impact
cards.answer: User numbers and revenue measured against the Enforcement Decree criteria
cards.why: The Act has three distinct triggers that are easy to swap: the compute threshold (b) triggers the safety-report duty, and high-impact designation (c) triggers risk-management duties — the representative duty keys on user/revenue scale for foreign operators.
cards.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); Cooley — South Korea's AI Basic Act

cards.q: A deficiency notice cites the way your service marks generative output. Which instrument sets out how marking must actually be done in Korea?
options: The Enforcement Decree of the AI Basic Act
The METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business
cards.answer: The Enforcement Decree of the AI Basic Act
cards.why: GB 45438-2025 is China's mandatory labelling standard and the METI/MIC guidelines are Japan's voluntary layer — Korea's labelling methods are detailed in the Enforcement Decree, finalized and effective with the Act on 2026-01-22 after the September 2025 draft.
cards.citation: Enforcement Decree of the AI Basic Act; FPF — South Korea's New AI Framework Act

cards.q: In an audit, MSIT probes whether your system should have been treated as high-impact all along. What determines that status?
options: MSIT's determination weighing usage extent and the severity and frequency of risk
Whether the use case appears on an enumerated high-risk annex
The operator's own designation, with no regulator involvement
cards.answer: MSIT's determination weighing usage extent and the severity and frequency of risk
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): an enumerated use-case annex is the EU's Annex III architecture — Korea uses criteria-based determination under the Enforcement Decree, which businesses report remains vague in practice.
cards.citation: Enforcement Decree of the AI Basic Act; Cooley — South Korea's AI Basic Act

cards.q: It is August 2026 and you operate in Korea. What is the realistic enforcement posture right now?
options: Fines up to KRW 30 million exist, but MSIT is running a grace period of at least a year — enforcement generally deferred except serious-harm cases
Full administrative fines have been levied since the Act's first day in force
The Act is not yet in force, so nothing can be enforced
cards.answer: Fines up to KRW 30 million exist, but MSIT is running a grace period of at least a year — enforcement generally deferred except serious-harm cases
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), which transplants the EU's deferred Annex III timeline onto Korea — the Framework Act has applied since 2026-01-22; what is soft-pedalled in 2026 is enforcement, not applicability. That distinction (in force vs actively fined) is exactly what a compliance brief must get right.
cards.citation: trade.gov — South Korea AI Basic Act (grace period, fines)

cards.q: You brief EU colleagues on Korea. How do the Framework Act's business categories map onto the EU AI Act's?
options: They don't map one-to-one: duties attach to 'AI business operators', subdivided into development and utilization operators that largely share duties
Korea copied provider, deployer and importer into its statute verbatim
Korea regulates only the business that develops AI; business users are out of scope
cards.answer: They don't map one-to-one: duties attach to 'AI business operators', subdivided into development and utilization operators that largely share duties
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the EU's provider/deployer/importer split allocates sharply different duty sets per role, and Korea rejected that design — its two operator types largely share obligations, and Korea's foreign-operator domestic-representative duty is threshold-based (user/revenue scale) where the EU's authorised-representative duty (Art. 22) is role-based, attaching to every third-country provider.
cards.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676); CSET official-text translation

cards.q: You want to launch a public-facing chatbot built on a large model in mainland China. Which instrument sets the baseline duties — training-data governance, content safety — for the service?
options: The Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services (CAC and six agencies)
The comprehensive AI law China enacted in 2026
The amended Cybersecurity Law on its own
The Model AI Governance Framework
cards.answer: The Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services (CAC and six agencies)
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): no unified AI statute exists in China as of August 2026 — comprehensive-law drafting has only been accelerated on the 2026 legislative agenda. (c) adds AI safe-development language but is not the operative service-level rulebook; (d) is Singapore's voluntary framework. The Interim Measures have been in force since 2023-08-15.
cards.citation: Interim Measures for Generative AI Services (CAC); White & Case — AI Watch China

cards.q: Before your recommendation and generation algorithms serve the Chinese public, what administrative step do China's algorithm provisions require?
options: File the algorithm with the CAC registry
Affix a conformity mark after a self-assessment against essential requirements
Obtain a court order authorising deployment
Publish the model weights for public inspection
cards.answer: File the algorithm with the CAC registry
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): self-assessment-plus-marking is the EU internal-control conformity route — China's mechanism is administrative filing in a regulator-run registry (Algorithm Recommendation Provisions, in force 2022-03-01), and public-facing generative services file too: 796 had completed filing as of 2026-02-28. Filing is not certification and not CE marking.
cards.citation: Algorithm Recommendation Provisions; ICLG 2026 — China AI governance developments

cards.q: Your product lets users swap faces in video for the Chinese market. Which rules first imposed consent, marking and filing duties on this technology — and what is their status now?
options: The Deep Synthesis Provisions (in force since January 2023) — still in force alongside the 2025 labelling measures
The Deep Synthesis Provisions, but they were repealed when the 2025 labelling measures took effect
The Interim Measures for generative services — deepfakes have no dedicated Chinese rules
GB 45438-2025 is the only instrument covering synthetic media
cards.answer: The Deep Synthesis Provisions (in force since January 2023) — still in force alongside the 2025 labelling measures
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the layering is the tested fact — China stacks instruments rather than replacing them, so the Deep Synthesis Provisions (eff. 2023-01-10) operate alongside the Labelling Measures and GB 45438-2025. Assuming the newer measure supersedes the older is the classic error in this regime.
cards.citation: Provisions on Deep Synthesis Internet Information Services; ICLG 2026 — China AI governance developments

cards.q: From September 2025, what must your generation service itself apply to synthetic output destined for Chinese users?
options: Both explicit visible labels and implicit metadata labels, per the Labelling Measures and mandatory standard GB 45438-2025
A visible label only where the content is realistic; machine-readable marks suffice for clearly artificial output
Marks only when a user requests them
Nothing — marking duties fall solely on the distribution platform
cards.answer: Both explicit visible labels and implicit metadata labels, per the Labelling Measures and mandatory standard GB 45438-2025
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the realistic-vs-clearly-artificial distinction is Korea's rule under its Framework Act — China requires BOTH label types on generated output regardless. (d) inverts the duty split: platforms have their own verify-and-relabel obligations, but that supplements rather than replaces the generator's duty.
cards.citation: Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Synthetic Content + GB 45438-2025 (eff. 2025-09-01)

cards.q: Your chatbot can shape public opinion at scale. Beyond registry paperwork, what pre-launch hurdle applies to public-facing services like this in China?
options: A security assessment under the Interim Measures before offering the service to the public
A notified-body conformity assessment
A fundamental rights impact assessment
A voluntary AI Verify test report
cards.answer: A security assessment under the Interim Measures before offering the service to the public
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): third-party conformity assessment is the EU's reserved route for certain biometric systems — China's gate for services with public-opinion attributes is a regulator-facing security assessment paired with filing. (c) is the EU deployer's FRIA; (d) is Singapore's voluntary assurance tooling.
cards.citation: Interim Measures for Generative AI Services (CAC); White & Case — AI Watch China

cards.q: A regulator audit letter targets your model's training corpus. Under the Interim Measures, what must you show about the data?
options: That sources were lawful — respecting intellectual property and personal-information rights
Only that the data was stored on servers inside China
Nothing — training data sits outside the scope of the generative-AI rules
cards.answer: That sources were lawful — respecting intellectual property and personal-information rights
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): data localisation is a Cybersecurity Law / Data Security Law concern — the Interim Measures' training-data governance duty is about source legality, IP and personal-information compliance, and training data is expressly in scope (contrary to (c)).
cards.citation: Interim Measures for Generative AI Services (CAC)

cards.q: An inspection finds your service's output stripped of its hidden marks when re-shared on a Chinese platform. Who must check and re-mark such content, and under what?
options: The distribution platform, which must verify and re-label under the Labelling Measures and GB 45438-2025
Only the original generation service — platforms carry no marking duties
No one — implicit marks are optional under Chinese law
cards.answer: The distribution platform, which must verify and re-label under the Labelling Measures and GB 45438-2025
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which describes Korea's operator-only duty design — China uniquely extends verification and re-labelling duties to distribution platforms. Implicit metadata labels are mandatory, not optional, so (c) fails too.
cards.citation: Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Synthetic Content + GB 45438-2025 (eff. 2025-09-01)

cards.q: A director asks whether China has 'an AI Act'. What is the accurate answer in August 2026?
options: No unified statute — a stack of binding sectoral measures (generative services, deep synthesis, recommendation algorithms, content labelling) governs instead
Yes — a comprehensive AI law took effect on 2026-01-01
No — AI in China is governed only by voluntary guidance
cards.answer: No unified statute — a stack of binding sectoral measures (generative services, deep synthesis, recommendation algorithms, content labelling) governs instead
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): what took effect on 2026-01-01 is the amended Cybersecurity Law with AI safe-development provisions — not a comprehensive AI statute. (c) confuses China with Japan or Singapore: China's measures are fully binding, just not consolidated.
cards.citation: State Council 2026 Legislative Work Plan; White & Case — AI Watch China

cards.q: What changed at the statute level in China during 2026, and what is on the horizon?
options: The amended Cybersecurity Law with AI safe-development provisions took effect 2026-01-01, and comprehensive-AI-law drafting was formally accelerated in the May 2026 legislative work plans
A comprehensive AI law was enacted in May 2026
Nothing — Chinese AI rulemaking is frozen pending the unified law
cards.answer: The amended Cybersecurity Law with AI safe-development provisions took effect 2026-01-01, and comprehensive-AI-law drafting was formally accelerated in the May 2026 legislative work plans
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the State Council's 'accelerate comprehensive legislation' commitment is a drafting agenda, not an enactment — no unified statute is in force as of 2026-08-02. The CSL amendment (adopted by the NPC Standing Committee 2025-10-28) is real but is an amendment to existing law, not the awaited AI act.
cards.citation: NPC — Cybersecurity Law amendment; State Council 2026 Legislative Work Plan

cards.q: Entering Japan, you ask counsel what the AI Promotion Act obliges your company to do. What is the accurate answer?
options: Nothing enforceable — the sole private-sector clause is a non-binding effort duty to cooperate, and the statute carries no penalties
Register high-risk systems with METI before deployment
Undergo third-party conformity assessment for generative systems
Nothing, because Japan has no AI legislation at all
cards.answer: Nothing enforceable — the sole private-sector clause is a non-binding effort duty to cooperate, and the statute carries no penalties
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d), the outdated claim: Japan HAS a binding statute — the AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025), in force since 2025-06-04 — it just imposes no business obligations. (b) and (c) import EU-style registration and conformity machinery that Japan deliberately never adopted.
cards.citation: AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025); Cabinet Office ai_act

cards.q: If Japan's statute imposes nothing on business, where does its operative AI governance actually live?
options: In the voluntary METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business, backed by existing laws such as the APPI, copyright and product liability
In binding Cabinet ordinances issued under the Promotion Act
In prefecture-level AI ordinances
In mandatory business codes issued by the AI Strategy Headquarters
cards.answer: In the voluntary METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business, backed by existing laws such as the APPI, copyright and product liability
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b)/(d): the Act does create government machinery — the AI Strategy Headquarters and the AI Basic Plan (adopted by Cabinet 2025-12-23) — but that machinery directs the state, not business. The operative layer for companies is agile, voluntary guidance riding on general law.
cards.citation: AI Guidelines for Business (METI/MIC); FPF — Understanding Japan's AI Promotion Act

cards.q: Under the Promotion Act, what CAN the Japanese government do about a company whose AI causes serious harm?
options: Investigate and publicly name malicious cases — but impose no fines
Levy administrative fines of up to 3% of global turnover
Suspend the service by ministerial order
Order a mandatory recall of the AI system
cards.answer: Investigate and publicly name malicious cases — but impose no fines
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): a 3%-of-turnover fining power is the EU Commission's GPAI enforcement tool — Japan's act contains no monetary penalties at all. Reputational naming after investigation is the only teeth; there is no suspension or recall power in the statute.
cards.citation: AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025); White & Case — Japan's first AI legislation

cards.q: Pin the dates: when did Japan's first AI statute pass and take effect?
options: Passed by the Diet 2025-05-28; main provisions in force 2025-06-04; institutional chapters 2025-09-01
Passed December 2025; in force January 2026
Still a pending bill as of August 2026
cards.answer: Passed by the Diet 2025-05-28; main provisions in force 2025-06-04; institutional chapters 2025-09-01
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), which is Taiwan's AI Basic Act timeline (passed 2025-12-23, effective 2026-01-14) — the two Asian framework statutes are easy to swap because they share the no-business-duties design.
cards.citation: AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025); e-Gov law text

cards.q: 'Japan has an AI law, so we need a compliance programme like our EU one.' What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: It equates having a statute with having obligations — Japan's act promotes and coordinates but binds only the state
Nothing — the statement is correct
It is wrong because Japan's AI law was repealed in 2026
cards.answer: It equates having a statute with having obligations — Japan's act promotes and coordinates but binds only the state
cards.why: The pattern recurs in Taiwan's Basic Act — statute in force, business duties absent — so 'has an AI law' is never sufficient for a compliance trigger. In Japan the trigger for companies remains general law (APPI, product liability), not the AI statute, and nothing was repealed.
cards.citation: AI Promotion Act (Act No. 53 of 2025); FPF — Understanding Japan's AI Promotion Act

cards.q: Which instruments actually bind your private-sector AI deployment in Australia?
options: Existing technology-neutral laws — privacy, consumer and anti-discrimination — enforced by sector regulators
The Voluntary AI Safety Standard, which became mandatory in 2025
The Australian AI Act passed alongside the National AI Plan
The mandatory AI requirements for Commonwealth agencies
cards.answer: Existing technology-neutral laws — privacy, consumer and anti-discrimination — enforced by sector regulators
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (d): the Commonwealth-agency requirements ARE binding (first requirements 2026-06-15) but only on federal agencies, never on the private sector. (b) and (c) never happened — the guidance stack stayed voluntary (the AI6 Guidance for AI Adoption superseded the 2024 standard in October 2025) and no AI act exists.
cards.citation: National AI Plan (Dec 2025); Guidance for AI Adoption (AI6)

cards.q: What did the December 2025 National AI Plan decide about the 2024 proposal for mandatory guardrails on high-risk AI?
options: It abandoned the proposal — no standalone AI act; reliance on existing law plus a new advisory AI Safety Institute
It scheduled the proposal's guardrails to commence in 2027
It converted the guardrails into a binding standard with immediate effect
It referred the guardrails to the states and territories to legislate
cards.answer: It abandoned the proposal — no standalone AI act; reliance on existing law plus a new advisory AI Safety Institute
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the stale-news trap: 2024 reporting made mandatory guardrails look inevitable, but the National AI Plan formally dropped them. The Australian AI Safety Institute (launched early 2026, AUD 29.9m) is advisory, not a regulator — no enforcement powers came with it.
cards.citation: National AI Plan (Dec 2025); Australia walks away from mandatory AI guardrails

cards.q: Australia does have binding AI rules starting June 2026 — for whom?
options: Commonwealth agencies only — impact assessments, accountable officials and training, phasing to full compliance by 2026-12-15
All deployers of high-risk AI nationwide
Foreign AI providers serving Australian users
cards.answer: Commonwealth agencies only — impact assessments, accountable officials and training, phasing to full compliance by 2026-12-15
cards.why: This government-internal DTA policy is the confusable that fuels 'Australia went mandatory' claims — it binds federal agencies as an administrative policy, while the private sector remains under voluntary guidance and general law. Note the date discipline: agency full compliance is 2026-12-15, distinct from the Privacy Act ADM date in December 2026.
cards.citation: DTA policy for responsible use of AI in government v2.0

cards.q: Which binding change lands on 10 December 2026 for Australian companies using automated decisions?
options: Privacy Act transparency obligations for automated decision-making commence (tranche-1 reform)
The AI Safety Institute gains enforcement powers
Mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI take effect
cards.answer: Privacy Act transparency obligations for automated decision-making commence (tranche-1 reform)
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the abandoned proposal — the December 2026 change comes from the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024, existing law adapting to AI, not an AI statute. The AI Safety Institute stays advisory; it gained no powers.
cards.citation: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (ADM transparency)
