cards.q: An adviser urges you to pre-comply now because Australia's mandatory AI guardrails 'are about to commence'. What is the true status?
options: Still voluntary — and the mandatory-guardrails proposal was formally dropped in the December 2025 National AI Plan
The adviser is right — the guardrails commence within months
Partly right — the guardrails bind only foreign providers
cards.answer: Still voluntary — and the mandatory-guardrails proposal was formally dropped in the December 2025 National AI Plan
cards.why: The adviser is working from stale 2024 reporting on the proposals paper. The only binding accents in Australia are government-internal agency rules (from 2026-06-15) and the Privacy Act ADM transparency change (December 2026) — neither is 'AI guardrails', and neither touches ordinary private-sector deployment.
cards.citation: National AI Plan (Dec 2025); Australia walks away from mandatory AI guardrails

cards.q: What is the legal weight of the India AI Governance Guidelines that MeitY released in November 2025?
options: An official but non-enforceable framework — light-touch and pro-innovation, with harms handled through existing law
Binding rules enforceable with penalties by MeitY
A draft that was never officially adopted
A state-level framework applying only in a few states
cards.answer: An official but non-enforceable framework — light-touch and pro-innovation, with harms handled through existing law
cards.why: The confusables are 'official' and 'binding' pulling in opposite directions: the Guidelines are genuinely government-issued (under the IndiaAI Mission) yet voluntary — India's binding instruments are general and sectoral laws (DPDP, IT Rules), never the Guidelines themselves.
cards.citation: MeitY India AI Governance Guidelines (Nov 2025)

cards.q: Your model trains on Indian users' personal data. Which binding regime governs that today, and where is it in its rollout?
options: The DPDP Act, with Rules notified 2025-11-13 — phased, with core data-fiduciary duties landing around mid-2027
The Artificial Intelligence (Ethics and Accountability) Act, in force since December 2025
No binding regime — India relies wholly on voluntary guidelines
The EU GDPR, applied extraterritorially to Indian residents
cards.answer: The DPDP Act, with Rules notified 2025-11-13 — phased, with core data-fiduciary duties landing around mid-2027
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): that bill is a private member's bill introduced in the Lok Sabha in December 2025, not enacted law. The DPDP regime is not AI-specific, but its consent requirements reach personal data used for model training — which is exactly why (c) is wrong.
cards.citation: DPDP Rules 2025 (notified 2025-11-13); AZB — DPDP phased rollout

cards.q: Does India have any binding AI-specific rules in force in August 2026?
options: Yes — the IT Amendment Rules 2026 require intermediaries to prominently label synthetically generated content, in force since 2026-02-20
Yes — a comprehensive AI statute took effect in 2026
No — everything AI-related in India is voluntary
Yes — the MeitY Guidelines became binding during 2026
cards.answer: Yes — the IT Amendment Rules 2026 require intermediaries to prominently label synthetically generated content, in force since 2026-02-20
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), over-applying India's 'voluntary' label: accurate for the horizontal framework, but the deepfake-labelling rules under the IT Act (Gazette notification February 2026) are binding and AI-specific — user declarations, prominent labels, provenance metadata where feasible. No comprehensive AI statute exists and the Guidelines never hardened.
cards.citation: IT Amendment Rules 2026 (G.S.R. 120(E), in force 2026-02-20)

cards.q: Summarise India's AI-governance position correctly for a board briefing.
options: Voluntary horizontal guidelines, a binding general data-protection regime phasing in, and binding synthetic-content rules — but no AI statute
A single AI Act covering all of it since 2025
No official position at all — India has not addressed AI governance
cards.answer: Voluntary horizontal guidelines, a binding general data-protection regime phasing in, and binding synthetic-content rules — but no AI statute
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), the old 'none' classification — outdated since MeitY's official framework of November 2025. India is a layered regime, not a statute regime: what binds is general law (DPDP) and sectoral rules (IT Amendment Rules), while the AI-wide layer stays voluntary.
cards.citation: MeitY India AI Governance Guidelines (Nov 2025); DPDP Rules 2025

cards.q: The 'Artificial Intelligence (Ethics and Accountability) Bill, 2025' appears in your India news scan. How should you weight it?
options: Low — a private member's bill introduced in the Lok Sabha in December 2025, not enacted and unlikely to pass
High — bills of this kind are typically enacted within months
It already passed and takes effect in 2027
cards.answer: Low — a private member's bill introduced in the Lok Sabha in December 2025, not enacted and unlikely to pass
cards.why: The discriminator is private member's bill versus government instrument: contrast the DPDP Rules, which MeitY notified and which ARE binding and phasing in. Treating every introduced bill as pending law is the horizon-scanning error this card trains against.
cards.citation: AI (Ethics and Accountability) Bill 2025 — Lok Sabha private member's bill

cards.q: Singapore's flagship AI-governance instruments carry what legal force?
options: None — the Model AI Governance Framework and its GenAI edition are voluntary
Binding on all AI developers through the PDPA
Binding once a company self-certifies against them
Mandatory for government vendors only
cards.answer: None — the Model AI Governance Framework and its GenAI edition are voluntary
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the PDPA is binding law, but it is general data protection — the Model Framework (2nd ed. 2020) and GenAI edition (May 2024) sit on top of it voluntarily. No self-certification mechanism converts them into obligations; Singapore is the deliberate voluntary exemplar.
cards.citation: Model AI Governance Framework + GenAI edition; GLI 2026 — Singapore

cards.q: What is AI Verify, and what does using it commit your company to?
options: An open-source testing framework and toolkit — process checks plus technical tests, with no legal commitment
A government licensing scheme for AI deployment
Singapore's mandatory conformity-assessment body
A binding audit standard issued under MAS FEAT
cards.answer: An open-source testing framework and toolkit — process checks plus technical tests, with no legal commitment
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c): 'conformity assessment' is EU-route thinking — AI Verify (IMDA, open-sourced 2023 under the AI Verify Foundation) is voluntary assurance tooling, not a gatekeeper. MAS FEAT (d) is sectoral guidance for financial institutions and is likewise non-binding.
cards.citation: AI Verify testing framework + toolkit (IMDA / AI Verify Foundation)

cards.q: In January 2026 at Davos, IMDA launched a world-first governance instrument. For what technology, and with what force?
options: Agentic AI — a voluntary Model framework, the first of its kind anywhere
Agentic AI — binding rules with penalties
Generative AI — that edition was the 2026 launch
Autonomous vehicles — a mandatory certification scheme
cards.answer: Agentic AI — a voluntary Model framework, the first of its kind anywhere
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (c), a date slip: the GenAI edition dates from May 2024 — the 2026-01-22 Davos launch was the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI, non-binding like the rest of Singapore's stack (and updated with industry feedback on 2026-05-20).
cards.citation: IMDA — Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (2026-01-22)

cards.q: Where do binding obligations for your Singapore AI deployment actually come from?
options: Existing general laws — the PDPA and sectoral regimes — with regulators issuing AI guidance under them
The Model AI Governance Framework, once IMDA endorses your use case
AI Verify test reports filed with IMDA
cards.answer: Existing general laws — the PDPA and sectoral regimes — with regulators issuing AI guidance under them
cards.why: The confusable is mistaking sector guidance (MAS FEAT/Veritas, MOH healthcare guidelines) for standalone AI law — that guidance interprets existing binding statutes; the AI-specific layer itself never binds. There is no IMDA endorsement or filing mechanism that creates obligations.
cards.citation: GLI 2026 — Singapore; Mayer Brown mid-year checkpoint 2026

cards.q: On 22 January 2026, two Asian jurisdictions made AI-governance news on the same day. What is the contrast?
options: Korea's binding AI Framework Act entered into force while Singapore launched another voluntary framework — for agentic AI
Both enacted binding AI statutes that day
Singapore enacted a binding statute while Korea launched voluntary guidance
cards.answer: Korea's binding AI Framework Act entered into force while Singapore launched another voluntary framework — for agentic AI
cards.why: The trap is the reversal in (c) — Singapore is the voluntary exemplar and Korea the comprehensive-law jurisdiction. The date coincidence makes a clean memory anchor for Asia's two diverging governance tracks.
cards.citation: IMDA — Agentic AI framework press release; AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676)

cards.q: What is the status of Taiwan's AI Basic Act in August 2026?
options: Passed on third reading 2025-12-23, promulgated and in force since 2026-01-14
Still the stalled 2024 NSTC draft, not yet passed
Passed, but not effective until sector rules issue
Vetoed by the President in January 2026
cards.answer: Passed on third reading 2025-12-23, promulgated and in force since 2026-01-14
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the outdated claim — the bill did stall for years as the NSTC draft, but the Legislative Yuan passed it in December 2025 and President Lai promulgated it effective 2026-01-14. (c) confuses the statute's effectiveness with the arrival of business duties: the Act took effect on promulgation; the duties are what await sector rules.
cards.citation: MODA press release; LoC Global Legal Monitor — Taiwan AI Basic Act

cards.q: Your Taipei subsidiary asks which agency it will ultimately answer to under the AI Basic Act, and which one owes it the coming risk framework. The correct split is:
options: The NSTC is the central competent authority; MODA is tasked with building the risk-classification framework
MODA is the central competent authority; the NSTC drafts the risk framework
A newly created dedicated AI commission holds both roles
Each sector regulator is its own central authority — there is no centre
cards.answer: The NSTC is the central competent authority; MODA is tasked with building the risk-classification framework
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the exact inversion — MODA is the digital ministry and looks like the natural lead, but the Act seats central competence with the science and technology council (NSTC) and delegates the internationally aligned risk-classification framework to MODA (Q1 2026 target, slipping). No new AI commission exists (c), and sector regulators (d) act only under the coming framework.
cards.citation: AI Basic Act (promulgated 2026-01-14); LoC Global Legal Monitor — Taiwan AI Basic Act

cards.q: What does Taiwan's AI Basic Act actually contain?
options: Seven governance principles, NSTC as central authority, MODA tasked with a risk framework, and implementing measures due within 24 months
A high-risk use-case annex with conformity-assessment requirements
Fines of up to NT$30 million for non-compliant developers
A licensing regime for foundation models
cards.answer: Seven governance principles, NSTC as central authority, MODA tasked with a risk framework, and implementing measures due within 24 months
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): an enumerated high-risk annex with conformity assessment is the EU AI Act's architecture — Taiwan chose principles-plus-delegation instead (sustainability, human autonomy, privacy, security, transparency, fairness, accountability). The Act contains no fines on business and no licensing.
cards.citation: MODA press release; LoC Global Legal Monitor — Taiwan AI Basic Act

cards.q: Which other jurisdiction's approach does Taiwan's Basic Act most resemble, and why?
options: Japan's — a binding framework statute in force that imposes no business obligations or penalties
Korea's — comprehensive operator duties applying from day one
The EU's — enforceable risk tiers with provider obligations
cards.answer: Japan's — a binding framework statute in force that imposes no business obligations or penalties
cards.why: The tempting neighbour-match (b) is the opposite pattern: Korea's Framework Act carries operative duties, fines and extraterritorial reach from commencement. Taiwan and Japan share the statute-without-business-duties design — law on the books, obligations delegated to the future.
cards.citation: AI Basic Act (promulgated 2026-01-14); Baker McKenzie — Taiwan AI Basic Act

cards.q: When should you expect business-facing AI obligations in Taiwan, and from where?
options: Via MODA's risk-classification framework and sector rules — the Act gives a 24-month window for implementing measures, to roughly early 2028
They took effect together with the Act in January 2026
Never — the Act forecloses sectoral AI regulation
cards.answer: Via MODA's risk-classification framework and sector rules — the Act gives a 24-month window for implementing measures, to roughly early 2028
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b), the statute-equals-duties error this territory exists to break. The compliance action today is monitoring: the MODA risk framework had a Q1 2026 public target that appears to be slipping, and sector regulators legislate only after it lands.
cards.citation: AI Basic Act (promulgated 2026-01-14); MODA press release

cards.q: Your client operates credit-scoring AI from the DIFC in Dubai and asks what binding AI-specific rules apply in August 2026. What is the correct scope answer?
options: Regulation 10 of the DIFC data-protection regime — duties for autonomous and semi-autonomous systems, enforced in full since January 2026
A horizontal UAE federal AI act applying across all seven emirates
The UAE AI Charter, which imposes twelve enforceable obligations
No rules at all — the UAE governs AI purely by strategy documents
cards.answer: Regulation 10 of the DIFC data-protection regime — duties for autonomous and semi-autonomous systems, enforced in full since January 2026
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): no horizontal UAE AI statute exists — the June 2026 federal body is a regulator, not an act. (c) inverts the Charter, which is aspirational. (d) ignores that one binding instrument does exist, but only inside the financial free zone.
cards.citation: DIFC Data Protection Regulations, Regulation 10 (full enforcement from 2026-01-01)

cards.q: In June 2026 Sheikh Mohammed announced a major federal AI initiative. What did it actually create?
options: A unified federal regulator for AI, digital government and data — an institutional step, with no horizontal AI statute attached
A binding federal AI act with penalties effective immediately
An extension of the DIFC's autonomous-systems rules to the whole country
A voluntary industry council with no regulatory mandate
cards.answer: A unified federal regulator for AI, digital government and data — an institutional step, with no horizontal AI statute attached
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — regulator is not statute: the 2026-06-14 announcement created the Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, while the UAE still has no horizontal AI law. (c) is wrong because Regulation 10 stays scoped to the DIFC free zone.
cards.citation: Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data (announced 2026-06-14)

cards.q: Procurement asks whether the UAE Charter for the Development and Use of AI creates compliance obligations for your product. What is the correct answer?
options: No — twelve aspirational principles with no enforcement machinery behind them
Yes — it carries the same fines as the DIFC's autonomous-systems rules
Yes, but only for government entities in Abu Dhabi
No, because it was repealed when the federal AI authority was announced
cards.answer: No — twelve aspirational principles with no enforcement machinery behind them
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the instrument with real fines (about USD 25k–50k per violation) is DIFC Regulation 10, not the Charter (July 2024), which has no enforcement arm. (d) invents a repeal — the Charter simply sits alongside the new authority.
cards.citation: UAE Charter for the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence (July 2024)

cards.q: The DIFC Commissioner questions your autonomous credit-decisioning deployment. Which duty cluster must your response evidence?
options: Impact assessment, transparency notices, documentation and audit or certification duties
CE marking backed by an EU declaration of conformity
A published bias-audit summary under the municipal hiring rule
cards.answer: Impact assessment, transparency notices, documentation and audit or certification duties
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — CE marking and declarations of conformity are EU AI Act artifacts with no DIFC counterpart. (c) is NYC Local Law 144's employer duty. Regulation 10 asks for the data-protection-style cluster, with fines around USD 25k–50k per violation.
cards.citation: DIFC Data Protection Regulations, Regulation 10

cards.q: Your mainland Dubai operation — outside the free zone — receives a regulator letter about its algorithmic processing of customers. Which regime is actually in play?
options: The federal data-protection law's automated-decision provisions — the zone-scoped AI rule stops at the zone boundary
DIFC Regulation 10, which has applied UAE-wide since January 2026
The UAE AI Charter's enforcement chapter
cards.answer: The federal data-protection law's automated-decision provisions — the zone-scoped AI rule stops at the zone boundary
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): January 2026 changed enforcement intensity, not geography — Regulation 10 binds only within the DIFC. The Charter (c) has no enforcement chapter. Mainland processing answers to PDPL (Decree-Law 45/2021), with a reported 2027-01-01 compliance deadline.
cards.citation: UAE PDPL (Federal Decree-Law 45/2021), automated-decision provisions

cards.q: Why does the UAE sit in the sectoral band of your compliance map when it has no AI-specific statute for most of the country?
options: Its only binding AI rules are scoped to a financial free zone — defined by a place, not an industry
Because federal law imposes AI duties on the banking industry nationwide
Because the AI Charter binds the technology industry
cards.answer: Its only binding AI rules are scoped to a financial free zone — defined by a place, not an industry
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — there is no nationwide AI-specific banking duty; the binding instrument is DIFC Regulation 10 inside the zone, and even ADGM next door has only guidance, no Regulation-10 equivalent. (c) fails because the Charter binds no one.
cards.citation: DIFC Regulation 10; ADGM Data Protection Regulations 2021 (guidance only for AI)

cards.q: It is August 2026 and a client asks about the legal position of Kenya's Artificial Intelligence Bill. What is accurate?
options: It had its Senate first reading in April 2026 and sits in committee — it must still pass the National Assembly before assent
It was enacted and its licensing duties are already enforceable
It was withdrawn after criticism that it restricted political speech
It exists only as a ministry white paper, never introduced in parliament
cards.answer: It had its Senate first reading in April 2026 and sits in committee — it must still pass the National Assembly before assent
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the classic proposed-tier trap: Senate Bill No. 4 (published 2026-02-19, first reading 2026-04-02) is at committee stage, not law. (c) gets the criticism right but the withdrawal wrong; (d) understates a real bill before the Senate.
cards.citation: The Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Senate Bill No. 4); first reading 2026-04-02

cards.q: If Kenya's 2026 AI bill became law tomorrow, what regulatory shape would companies face?
options: An Office of the AI Commissioner licensing AI systems under risk-based provisions with penalties
An EU-style chain of provider, deployer and importer obligations
A voluntary code administered by the communications authority
Sector regulators issuing binding measures under a framework statute
cards.answer: An Office of the AI Commissioner licensing AI systems under risk-based provisions with penalties
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the bill regulates AI systems through a commissioner-licensing model and draws no EU-style role chain — its published text makes no clear provider/deployer distinction. (d) is the Taiwan pattern (and roughly Peru's), not Kenya's commissioner-licensing design.
cards.citation: The Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Senate Bill No. 4) — Office of the AI Commissioner

cards.q: While the AI bill waits in parliament, what actually steers AI governance in Kenya today?
options: The National AI Strategy 2025–2030, backed by a five-year implementation budget
The AI Commissioner's interim licensing regulations
Directly applicable African Union AI regulations
cards.answer: The National AI Strategy 2025–2030, backed by a five-year implementation budget
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): the Commissioner's office does not exist yet — it is created only if the bill passes. The African Union (c) issues continental strategy, not directly applicable regulation. The March 2025 strategy (about KES 152bn) is the operative framework.
cards.citation: Kenya National AI Strategy 2025-2030 (launched March 2025)

cards.q: Your Africa market brief must name the jurisdiction furthest along toward a standalone national AI statute. Why does Kenya top the list?
options: It has the only dedicated national AI bill before an African legislature in 2026 — peers govern by policy, strategy or broader digital-economy bills
It enacted Africa's first AI act in 2025
It adopted the EU AI Act wholesale through a trade agreement
cards.answer: It has the only dedicated national AI bill before an African legislature in 2026 — peers govern by policy, strategy or broader digital-economy bills
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b): nothing is enacted — a first-reading bill is precisely what puts Kenya ahead on the dedicated-statute track. Nigeria is the closest call, but its AI provisions sit inside a digital-economy omnibus (the e-governance bill, at third reading in July 2026), not a standalone AI act; Rwanda and South Africa govern by policy only. (c) invents an adoption mechanism that does not exist.
cards.citation: The Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Senate Bill No. 4); regional status per verified fact base

cards.q: An adviser warns that Singapore's new agentic-AI framework means autonomous agents are now legally regulated there. How do you respond?
options: Decline to pre-comply on that basis — it is voluntary guidance, and no binding AI-specific statute exists there
Agree — IMDA instruments carry penalties once launched at ministerial level
Agree in part — it binds agent operators but not developers
cards.answer: Decline to pre-comply on that basis — it is voluntary guidance, and no binding AI-specific statute exists there
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — launch profile is not legal force: the Davos debut (2026-01-22) and the 2026-05-20 update change nothing about the instrument being a voluntary IMDA model framework. (c) invents a role split; it addresses developers, deployers and agent operators without binding any of them.
cards.citation: IMDA — Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (launched 2026-01-22, updated 2026-05-20)

cards.q: Headline: 'Taiwan's AI law takes effect.' Leadership asks whether your Taipei business now needs a compliance programme. What is the correct call?
options: Not yet — the statute directs government action; obligations for firms arrive only through future risk-classification and sector measures
Yes — a framework act in force means operational duties and penalties apply now
Yes — Taiwan mirrored the EU AI Act, so provider duties began at once
cards.answer: Not yet — the statute directs government action; obligations for firms arrive only through future risk-classification and sector measures
cards.why: The nearest confusable is (b) — the statute-equals-duties error: the Basic Act (effective on promulgation, 2026-01-14) codifies seven principles and tasks MODA with a risk framework, imposing no immediate obligations or penalties on private business. (c) is wrong twice over: no EU mirroring, and no provider/deployer split yet.
cards.citation: Taiwan AI Basic Act (promulgated and effective 2026-01-14); MODA risk framework pending

events.title: Coordinated GPAI inquiry
events.text: The AI Office opens a coordinated inquiry into general-purpose model providers — and since the Digital Omnibus it wields real fining powers over GPAI providers (up to 3% of global turnover or EUR 15M). Your model documentation is requested.

events.title: Biometric-practice probe
events.text: A market-surveillance authority probes whether your biometric deployment crosses into the EU's prohibited-practices tier — the ban layer has applied since February 2025.

events.title: Incident-readiness sweep
events.text: A hospital customer reports a malfunction. The AI Office runs a readiness sweep: your post-market monitoring and serious-incident process will be duties when the deferred high-risk regime binds from 2 December 2027 — regulators are checking preparedness now.

events.title: GDPR Art-22 ADM complaint
events.text: A rejected loan applicant files an automated-decision-making complaint. Whatever the AI-law timeline says, GDPR Article 22 rights are enforceable today, and your DPO owns the response.

events.title: AEDT audit sweep
events.text: New York City's enforcement arm sweeps employers using automated employment decision tools: bias-audit currency and candidate notices are being checked.

events.title: Illinois HRA charge filed
events.text: A candidate files a Human Rights Act charge over AI use in hiring — the HB 3773 amendment has been in force since 1 January 2026, and the agency wants your records.

events.title: FTC AI-washing sweep
events.text: The FTC announces a deception sweep over exaggerated AI claims in consumer products. Your chatbot's marketing copy is in scope under Section 5.

events.title: ECOA adverse-action demand
events.text: A regulator demands your adverse-action notices for algorithmic credit denials — specific reasons are required, and 'the model said so' is not one.

events.title: California ADMT opt-out wave
events.text: Consumers exercise their California privacy rights against your automated decisionmaking in a coordinated wave. The ADMT regulations' access and opt-out machinery is being stress-tested on you.

events.title: SB 942 provenance spot-check
events.text: California spot-checks covered generative providers for AI-detection tooling and content disclosures under the AI Transparency Act.

events.title: Korea qualifying-threshold letter
events.text: The Ministry of Science and ICT writes: does your system meet the Framework Act's high-impact or compute thresholds? Misjudging scope here is the top Korea compliance failure.
events.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676, in force 2026-01-22)

events.title: Korea generative-labelling notice
events.text: A takedown notice cites unlabelled AI-generated output reaching Korean users. The Framework Act's generative-AI labelling duty is being enforced against your service.
events.citation: AI Framework Act (Act No. 20676) — generative labelling

events.title: CAC filing audit
events.text: The Cyberspace Administration audits your algorithm filing and security assessment for the public-facing generative service you operate in China.

events.title: Synthetic-content label inspection
events.text: Inspectors check your outputs for the explicit and implicit labels the 2025 labelling measures and their companion standard require on synthetic content.

events.title: DIFC autonomous-systems inspection
events.text: The DIFC Commissioner of Data Protection opens an inspection of your autonomous decision systems — Regulation 10 has been fully enforced since 1 January 2026, with per-violation fines.
events.citation: DIFC Data Protection Regulations, Regulation 10 (full enforcement 2026-01-01)

events.title: Peru reglamento verification
events.text: Peru's digital-government secretariat verifies your high-risk classification and duty evidence under Law 31814's implementing regulation, in force since January 2026.

events.title: You fine-tune a foundation model
events.text: Engineering ships a fine-tuned foundation model under your own brand. Congratulations: in EU terms you now carry provider duties for what you modified.
events.citation: Ch6 §GPAI; EU AI Act Art. 25 concept

events.title: White-label rebrand ships under your mark
events.text: Sales closes a white-label deal: a third-party system now ships under your trademark. Putting your name on it moves provider obligations onto you.
events.citation: EU AI Act Art. 25; Ch6 §Roles along the value chain

events.title: AIDA revival rumour
events.text: Ottawa insiders whisper that the federal AI bill — dead since prorogation killed Bill C-27 in January 2025 — is coming back. Clients want to know whether to stand up compliance now.
events.citation: ISED — AIDA (Bill C-27) companion document; prorogation 2025-01-06

events.title: Brazil Chamber momentum
events.text: Headlines say the Brazilian AI bill is moving in the Chamber of Deputies and an AI act is 'imminent'. A client asks whether to stand up an EU-style compliance programme in São Paulo this quarter.

events.title: Canberra guardrails headline
events.text: An Australian paper runs a mandatory-AI-rules headline. Worth remembering: the 2024 mandatory-guardrails proposal was abandoned in the December 2025 National AI Plan — check the substance before reacting.
events.citation: National AI Plan (Dec 2025) — mandatory guardrails proposal abandoned

events.title: Texas sandbox invitation
events.text: The Texas programme invites your novel AI product into its regulatory sandbox under TRAIGA. Getting the terms right earns supervised room to test.

events.title: EU regulatory-sandbox admission
events.text: A member-state sandbox — every member state must now have at least one operational — offers your novel system supervised testing with regulatory cover.

events.title: ISO/IEC 42001 certification opportunity
events.text: Your board wants a recognised credential for the AI management system before the next funding round. A certification audit window opens this quarter.

events.title: Comprehensive-regime enforcement sweep
events.text: Regulators in the binding-statute jurisdictions you operate across run a coordinated enforcement sweep. Knowing which duties are actually live where is the whole test.
events.citation: Cross-tier sweep — citation carried by the drawn card

events.title: Voluntary-framework benchmarking survey
events.text: An industry association benchmarks members against the voluntary frameworks of the soft-law jurisdictions you hold. Mislabelling what is and is not binding costs credibility.
events.citation: Cross-tier sweep — citation carried by the drawn card

events.text: After IMDA's world-first agentic-AI governance framework (launched at Davos, January 2026; updated May 2026), your board asks for a briefing on what it changes for your agents.
events.citation: IMDA — Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI (2026-01-22, updated 2026-05-20)

events.title: Taipei headline check
events.text: 'Taiwan's AI law is in force' crosses the wire and your leadership asks whether the Taipei business must now stand up a compliance programme. Read the statute before you answer.

events.title: Colorado moves the goalposts again
events.text: Colorado repealed SB 24-205 before it ever took effect and replaced it with SB 26-189 (signed 2026-05-14): a narrower ADMT disclosure law, effective 2027-01-01, with duties mainly on deployers. Date-churn is the lesson — track the law, not the headline.

events.title: Kenya bill reaches committee
events.text: Kenya's Artificial Intelligence Bill (Senate Bill No. 4) had its Senate first reading on 2 April 2026 and sits with the ICT committee. It must still pass the National Assembly — Africa's strongest dedicated-AI-bill candidate, but not yet law.
events.citation: The Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 (Senate Bill No. 4); first reading 2026-04-02

events.title: Swiss consultation opens
events.text: Switzerland stays deliberately minimalist: the Federal Council's February 2025 decision holds — lean, sectoral, no horizontal AI act — with a draft bill due in consultation by end-2026. The CoE Convention is signed but not ratified.
events.citation: Swiss Federal Council decision (Feb 2025); consultation draft due end-2026

events.title: Digital Omnibus reshuffles the deadlines
events.text: The June 2026 Digital Omnibus rewrote the EU AI Act timeline: Annex III high-risk duties now bind from 2 December 2027 (embedded systems 2028). Binding today: prohibitions and AI literacy, GPAI duties with fining powers, Article 50 transparency, and member-state sandboxes.

events.title: EU accedes to the Framework Convention
events.text: The EU's accession to the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI takes effect on 1 September 2026. Remember what kind of instrument this is: a binding treaty that binds states — obligations reach companies only through implementing law.
events.citation: CoE Framework Convention (in force 2025-11-01); EU accession effective 2026-09-01

events.title: Denver client asks about Colorado
events.text: A Denver client has read that Colorado passed an AI law and asks whether to stand up compliance now. Signing dates are not effective dates — check what actually binds today before you answer.

roleMatrix.title: Role Matrix
roleMatrix.prompt: Assign each obligation to the role it attaches to. Obligations follow actors, not systems.

sets.title: EU AI Act roles

roles.name: Provider
roles.definition: Develops an AI system or has one developed and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark.

roles.name: Deployer
roles.definition: Uses an AI system under its own authority, other than in a personal non-professional activity.

roles.name: Importer
roles.definition: Established in the EU and places on the market a system bearing the name or trademark of a third-country entity.

roles.name: Distributor
roles.definition: Makes a system available on the EU market without being provider or importer.

roles.name: Authorised representative
roles.definition: Appointed in writing by a third-country provider to act on its behalf in the EU.

obligations.text: Establish and maintain a risk management system across the lifecycle
Draw up technical documentation before placing on the market
Carry out the conformity assessment and affix CE marking
Register the high-risk system in the EU database
Operate a quality management system
Design the system so human oversight is possible
Apply data governance to training, validation and test data
Conduct post-market monitoring and report serious incidents
Use the system in accordance with the instructions for use
Assign human oversight to people with the competence and authority to act
Ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose
Inform workers and their representatives before putting a high-risk system into use in the workplace
Inform individuals that they are subject to a high-risk system's decision
Retain automatically generated logs for the required period
Carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment where required
Verify the provider has completed the conformity assessment before placing on the market
Verify the third-country provider has appointed an authorised representative
Indicate your name and contact address on the system or its packaging
Verify the CE marking and required documentation are present before making available
Refrain from making available a system you know or should know is non-compliant
Keep the declaration of conformity and technical documentation at the authorities' disposal
Terminate the mandate if the provider acts contrary to its obligations, and inform the authority

traps: A deployer becomes a provider by rebranding, substantially modifying, or changing the intended purpose so the system becomes high-risk.
Importer and distributor look similar: the importer brings a third-country system onto the EU market for the first time; the distributor moves one already on it.
Conformity assessment is never a deployer duty — but assigning competent human oversight is never a provider duty either. Providers design for oversight; deployers staff it.

sets.title: GDPR roles
sets.citation: Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations in the AI Context

roles.name: Controller
roles.definition: Determines the purposes and means of processing.

roles.name: Joint controllers
roles.definition: Two or more controllers that jointly determine purposes and means.

roles.name: Processor
roles.definition: Processes personal data on behalf of the controller.

roles.name: Data protection officer
roles.definition: Appointed to inform, advise and monitor compliance, independently.

roles.name: Article 27 representative
roles.definition: Represents a non-EU controller or processor within the EU.

obligations.text: Identify a lawful basis before processing begins
Provide Article 13 and 14 transparency information to data subjects
Respond to access, rectification, erasure and objection requests
Carry out a data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing
Notify the supervisory authority of a breach within 72 hours
Communicate a high-risk breach to affected data subjects
Put an Article 28 contract in place before engaging a processor
Establish a transfer mechanism under Chapter V before sending data abroad
Agree an arrangement setting out respective responsibilities, and make its essence available to data subjects
Accept that a data subject may exercise their rights against either of you, regardless of the arrangement
Process only on documented instructions from the controller
Obtain authorisation before engaging a sub-processor
Notify the controller of a personal data breach without undue delay
Assist the controller in responding to data subject requests
Delete or return the data at the end of the engagement
Inform and advise on obligations, and monitor compliance, without receiving instructions on how to perform the task
Act as the contact point for the supervisory authority and for data subjects
Maintain the record of processing activities and make it available to the authority on request

traps: A processor that starts determining purposes becomes a controller for that processing, whatever the contract says.
The DPO advises and monitors; the DPO does not own compliance and cannot be instructed how to do the job.
Security under Article 32 binds controller and processor alike — it is one of the few duties that genuinely sits on both.

sets.title: Where the AI Act and GDPR overlap
sets.citation: Ch4 §Practical Implications and Governance; Ch6 §Regulatory Intersection
sets.prompt: For each statement, decide whether it belongs to the EU AI Act, the GDPR, or both.

items.text: Roles are assigned by who places a system on the market or puts it into service
items.why: Market placement is the AI Act's allocator. The GDPR allocates by who determines purposes and means.

items.text: Roles are assigned by who determines the purposes and means of processing
An organisation can be a provider under one regime and a controller under the other for the same system
items.why: The two role sets are independent. A provider may process no personal data at all; a deployer is very often the controller.

items.text: Requires an impact assessment before high-risk activity
items.why: AI Act fundamental rights impact assessment for certain deployers; GDPR Article 35 DPIA for high-risk processing. Different triggers, different scopes, and they can be run together.

items.text: Gives an individual the right not to be subject to a solely automated decision with significant effects
items.why: Article 22 is a data subject right. The AI Act imposes oversight duties on organisations but does not create this right.

items.text: Requires that people be told when they are interacting with an AI system
items.why: Article 50 transparency. GDPR notice obligations are about processing of personal data, which is a different subject matter.

items.text: Applies to organisations outside the EU on the basis of effects inside it
items.why: Both reach extraterritorially, but on different triggers: market placement or output used in the EU, versus establishment, offering goods and services, or monitoring behaviour.

items.text: Maximum fines can reach 7% of total worldwide annual turnover
items.why: The Article 5 prohibitions band. The GDPR tops out at 4% or €20 million.

items.text: Permits processing special categories of data specifically to detect and correct bias, subject to safeguards
items.why: AI Act Article 10(5) creates the permission for high-risk bias monitoring; it has to be read with GDPR Article 9. Neither works alone.
The AI Act is enforced by market surveillance authorities and the AI Office — though some member states have designated their DPA as the market surveillance authority for certain Annex III areas.

items.text: Requires data used for training to be relevant, representative and as free of errors as possible
items.why: Article 10 data governance for high-risk systems. This sits in genuine tension with GDPR data minimisation, and reconciling the two is a governance judgment, not a lookup.

items.text: Requires records to be kept that demonstrate compliance
items.why: AI Act technical documentation, logging and record-keeping; GDPR Article 30 records and the Article 5(2) accountability principle.

items.text: Obligations can attach to you even if you never touch personal data
items.why: A provider of a high-risk system processing only industrial sensor data still carries the full obligation set. This is the cleanest demonstration that the two regimes are not nested.

traps: Complying with the GDPR does not discharge AI Act obligations, and vice versa. They stack, and so do the fines.
A fundamental rights impact assessment is not a renamed DPIA. They have different triggers and different scopes, even though they can be conducted together.
AI Act data governance pushes toward more and better data; GDPR minimisation pushes toward less. Naming that tension is what a real answer looks like.

cases.brief: A Dutch insurer licenses a third-party model to price motor policies, retrains it on its own claims history, and markets it to customers under its own brand. Pricing decisions are issued automatically.
cases.citation: Ch6 §When Deployers Become Providers; Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations

steps.q: What is the insurer under the EU AI Act?
options: Provider
Deployer
Importer
Distributor
steps.why: It rebranded the system and substantially modified it by retraining — either alone transfers provider obligations.

steps.q: Which additional regime is squarely engaged?
options: GDPR Article 22
Product liability
TDM exception
FTC Act §5
steps.why: Automatic pricing decisions with significant effects are solely automated decision-making.

steps.q: What must be in place before go-live?
options: Conformity assessment and technical documentation
A patent filing
An environmental report
A trade mark registration
steps.why: Provider duties for a high-risk system, alongside the DPIA required on the privacy side.

cases.brief: A US retailer's AI screening tool for warehouse roles rejects applicants at a much higher rate from one postal-code cluster that correlates strongly with race. There was no intent to discriminate.

options: Disparate impact
Disparate treatment
Breach of contract
Product defect
steps.why: Facially neutral feature, disproportionate effect, no intent needed.

steps.q: Which statute is the primary hook?
options: Title VII
ECOA
Fair Housing Act
FTC Act §5

steps.q: What is the employer's strongest defence posture?
options: Job-relatedness and business necessity, with a less discriminatory alternative assessed
The vendor built it
The feature was not race
Accuracy was high overall
steps.answer: Job-relatedness and business necessity, with a less discriminatory alternative assessed
steps.why: The statutory test. "The vendor built it" is not a defence, and overall accuracy does not answer disparate impact.

cases.brief: A board asks why the company should adopt ISO/IEC 42001 when it already intends to comply with the EU AI Act.

options: 42001 is a voluntary management system that can evidence AI Act compliance
42001 replaces AI Act obligations
42001 is binding law in the EU
They are unrelated
steps.answer: 42001 is a voluntary management system that can evidence AI Act compliance
steps.why: Standards are not law, but a certified management system is strong evidence of the governance the Act demands.

steps.q: What can 42001 do that the AI Act cannot?
options: Be certified by an accredited third party
Impose fines
Ban a practice
Confer legal immunity
steps.answer: Be certified by an accredited third party
steps.why: Certifiability is the practical value; it confers no immunity.

cases.brief: A US company trains a general-purpose model above the systemic-risk compute threshold. It has no EU establishment, but EU businesses integrate the model into their products.
cases.citation: Ch6 §Extraterritoriality; §Additional Obligations for GPAI with Systemic Risk

steps.q: Does the AI Act reach this provider?
options: Yes — the Act applies where output or the model is placed on the EU market
No — no EU establishment
Only if it has EU customers directly
Only after 2028
steps.answer: Yes — the Act applies where output or the model is placed on the EU market
steps.why: Extraterritorial reach follows market placement, not establishment.

options: Model evaluation, adversarial testing, incident reporting and cybersecurity
Nothing beyond baseline
Only a copyright policy
CE marking
steps.answer: Model evaluation, adversarial testing, incident reporting and cybersecurity
steps.why: Systemic-risk duties sit on top of the baseline GPAI set.

options: An authorised representative in the EU
A works council
A notified body
A data protection officer
steps.answer: An authorised representative in the EU
steps.why: Third-country GPAI providers must appoint an EU authorised representative.

cases.brief: A marketing agency fine-tunes an LLM on scraped web content to generate campaign copy. Some source sites carry machine-readable rights reservations. The campaign targets construction businesses, not individuals.
cases.citation: Ch5 §Intellectual Property Laws and AI; Ch4 §Notice, Choice, Consent

steps.q: What does the rights reservation mean for the training data?
options: The commercial TDM exception is unavailable, so a licence is needed
Reservations are unenforceable
Fair use applies automatically in the EU
Only attribution is required
steps.answer: The commercial TDM exception is unavailable, so a licence is needed
steps.why: The commercial exception can be reserved; the research exception cannot.

steps.q: Does GDPR apply to the targeting?
options: Not to business entities as such, but it does to identifiable contacts
Yes, fully, to companies
No, never to B2B
Only if consent was collected
steps.answer: Not to business entities as such, but it does to identifiable contacts
steps.why: Legal persons are outside GDPR, but named individuals at those firms are personal data.

cases.brief: It is September 2026. Your board asks which EU AI Act obligations currently bind the company's Annex III recruitment system.

currency.book: High-risk obligations would be in force from 2 August 2026.
currency.changed: The Digital Omnibus deferred standalone Annex III to 2 December 2027, so in September 2026 the full high-risk set does not yet bind. Article 50 transparency does, from 2 August 2026.
currency.exam: BoK v2.1 predates the Omnibus — for the exam, assume the enacted timeline.

steps.q: Which obligations are live in September 2026 on the amended timeline?
options: Article 50 transparency and the Article 5 prohibitions
The full high-risk conformity set
Nothing yet
Only GPAI duties
steps.answer: Article 50 transparency and the Article 5 prohibitions
steps.why: Prohibitions since February 2025, transparency since August 2026; high-risk deferred to December 2027.

steps.q: What is the right governance posture on the deferred obligations?
options: Continue preparing to the original schedule
Stop the programme
Wait for national guidance before acting
Reclassify the system as minimal risk
steps.answer: Continue preparing to the original schedule
steps.why: A deferral is not a repeal, and conformity work takes longer than the extension granted.

briefs.title: The support transcripts
briefs.scenario:
Helio, a SaaS company headquartered in Berlin, has eleven years of customer support transcripts — roughly 40 million messages. Customers were told at collection that the data would be used to "resolve your support request and improve our service". Helio's new product team wants to fine-tune a language model on the full archive to build an automated support agent, and later to license that agent to other companies.

The archive is not clean. Customers routinely paste screenshots, order numbers, and occasionally health information when explaining why they missed a payment. About 12% of transcripts come from users who have since closed their accounts, and 3% from users who have made erasure requests that were actioned against the account record but not against the transcript store. The transcripts are stored in Frankfurt, but the fine-tuning would run on infrastructure in Oregon.

The product team's position is that the transcripts are Helio's own business records, that "improve our service" covers building a better support agent, and that because the model will not reproduce transcripts verbatim, no personal data leaves the training process. The general counsel is uneasy but cannot articulate why. You are asked for a written position before the sprint starts.

fields.prompt: Is "improve our service" a sufficient basis for this training, and for the licensing plan?
fields.hint: Address purpose limitation and compatibility separately for each of the two uses.

fields.prompt: How do you handle the closed accounts and the 3% erasure requests?
What follows from the incidental health information in the transcripts?
What does the Frankfurt-to-Oregon training run require?
What controls and documentation would you require before the sprint starts?
State your position to the general counsel in five sentences or fewer.

rubric.criterion: Separates the two purposes
rubric.expected: Internal service improvement and commercial licensing to third parties are different purposes with different compatibility analyses. Licensing is very hard to bring inside the original notice.
rubric.citation: Ch4 §Notice, Choice, Consent, and Purpose Limitation in AI

rubric.criterion: Applies the compatibility test rather than asserting it
rubric.expected: Link to original purpose, context of collection, nature of the data, consequences, safeguards — not simply 'improve our service covers it'.
rubric.citation: Ch4 §Notice, Choice, Consent, and Purpose Limitation in AI

rubric.criterion: Treats erasure as extending to the training corpus
rubric.expected: Actioning erasure against the account record but not the transcript store is an incomplete response; the transcripts must be removed before training, and model memorisation risk addressed.
rubric.citation: Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations in the AI Context

rubric.criterion: Identifies incidental special-category data
rubric.expected: Art. 9 applies to health data even when incidental and unsolicited; needs an Art. 9 condition or robust filtering, and 'we did not ask for it' is not a basis.
rubric.citation: Ch4 §Understanding the Requirements That Apply to Sensitive or Special Categories of Data

rubric.criterion: Addresses the transfer properly
rubric.expected: Training in Oregon is a cross-border transfer requiring a Chapter V mechanism and a transfer risk assessment; storage location does not settle it.
rubric.citation: Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations in the AI Context

rubric.criterion: Rejects the 'no verbatim output' argument
rubric.expected: Training on personal data is processing regardless of whether outputs reproduce it; memorisation and extraction risk are additional concerns, not the test.

rubric.criterion: Requires a DPIA
rubric.expected: Large-scale processing of a decade of customer data including special categories for a new purpose meets the Art. 35 threshold.
rubric.citation: Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations in the AI Context

briefs.title: The hiring funnel
briefs.scenario:
Marchetti Logistics runs 400 warehouses across the United States and hires around 30,000 seasonal staff each year. To cope, it has deployed a third-party AI screening tool that scores applicants on a 0–100 "reliability index" built from work history, commute distance, prior seasonal completion rates, and a short situational judgement questionnaire. Anyone below 55 is auto-rejected without human review. The vendor describes the model as "bias-tested and EEOC-aligned" but will not disclose the feature weights, calling them proprietary.

Six months in, an internal analyst notices that applicants from three postal-code clusters are rejected at roughly 2.4 times the rate of others. Those clusters are predominantly Black and Hispanic. Commute distance is by far the heaviest-weighted feature. Separately, the tool has been marketed to Marchetti's own clients as a service, and Marchetti's website advertises it as "removing human bias from hiring".

Marchetti's operations director argues that commute distance is a legitimate business factor because long commutes predict no-shows, that the vendor certified the tool, and that no protected characteristic is used as an input. The head of HR wants to keep using it through peak season and review afterwards. You are the AI governance lead.

fields.prompt: What is the legal exposure, and under which statutes?
Is "commute distance predicts no-shows" a valid defence? Reason it through.
What is the significance of the vendor's certification and refusal to disclose weights?
Does the "removes human bias" claim create separate exposure?
Respond to the proposal to keep using it through peak season.
What would you require, in what order, and on what timescale?

rubric.criterion: Names disparate impact under Title VII
rubric.expected: Facially neutral criterion, disproportionate effect on protected groups, no intent required. Absence of protected characteristics as inputs is not a defence.

rubric.criterion: Applies the business necessity test, not a plausibility test
rubric.expected: Predictive validity is not sufficient; the employer must show job-relatedness and business necessity AND that no less discriminatory alternative achieving the same aim exists.

rubric.criterion: Identifies commute distance as a proxy
rubric.expected: Given US residential segregation, commute distance is a well-recognised race proxy; heaviest weighting on a proxy is the core defect.

rubric.criterion: Rejects vendor certification as a shield
rubric.expected: The employer remains liable for its own hiring decisions. Refusal to disclose weights is itself a governance failure and a contracting problem to fix.

rubric.criterion: Spots the consumer-protection exposure
rubric.expected: "Removes human bias" is an unsubstantiated performance claim under FTC Act §5 — and is now demonstrably false, which sharply increases exposure.
rubric.citation: Ch5 §How Consumer Protection Laws Apply to AI

rubric.criterion: Notes the role change from deployer to provider
rubric.expected: Marketing the tool onward to clients changes Marchetti's role and adds obligations and liability it does not have as a pure user.
rubric.citation: Ch5 §How Consumer Protection Laws Apply to AI

rubric.criterion: Refuses continued use of an auto-reject without human review
rubric.expected: Continuing knowingly after discovering the disparity converts a defensible mistake into aggravated exposure. Auto-rejection below threshold with no human review is the specific feature to suspend first.

rubric.criterion: Flags state-law exposure
rubric.expected: Illinois HB 3773 and NYC Local Law 144 impose notice and bias-audit duties on AI in employment; a national footprint means checking state overlays.
rubric.citation: Horizon — not in the study guide

briefs.title: NordBank AI Advisor
briefs.scenario:
NordBank, headquartered in Stockholm, licenses a general-purpose model from a US developer with no EU establishment. NordBank fine-tunes the model on twelve years of its own customer transaction data, wraps it in a decisioning layer, and deploys it to make consumer credit decisions across the Nordics and Germany. It is marketed to customers as "NordBank AI Advisor". Declines under €10,000 are issued automatically; above that, a credit officer reviews a one-line summary and, in practice, follows the recommendation 97% of the time.

The US developer's model was trained above the systemic-risk compute threshold. NordBank's contract with the developer disclaims all liability for downstream use and provides no technical documentation beyond a public model card. NordBank has not performed a conformity assessment; its position is that it is "only a customer" of the model. It plans to offer the Advisor to two smaller partner banks next year.

A declined customer has asked, in writing, how the decision about her was reached and what data was used. The board wants to know its exposure before the partner-bank rollout.

fields.prompt: What is NordBank under the EU AI Act, and what is the US developer? Justify each.
What is the risk classification of the Advisor, and on what basis?
Which obligations attach to NordBank, and which to the developer?
Which other regimes are engaged, and what do they require here?
How must NordBank answer the declined customer?
Quantify the exposure and state what must happen before the partner-bank rollout.

rubric.criterion: Identifies NordBank as provider, not deployer
rubric.expected: Own branding plus fine-tuning plus a new intended purpose — any one would suffice. "Only a customer" is wrong and is the central error.

rubric.criterion: Classifies as Annex III high-risk
rubric.expected: Creditworthiness evaluation of natural persons is expressly Annex III high-risk.

rubric.criterion: Rejects the human-review argument on the facts
rubric.expected: 97% concurrence on a one-line summary is rubber-stamping, not meaningful human oversight, so Art. 22 is engaged above €10,000 too.

rubric.criterion: Separates provider duties from GPAI duties
rubric.expected: NordBank owes the high-risk set (risk management, data governance, technical documentation, conformity assessment, CE marking, registration, human oversight, logging, quality management). The developer owes GPAI plus systemic-risk duties and must appoint an EU authorised representative.

rubric.criterion: Treats the contract as inadequate rather than protective
rubric.expected: A liability disclaimer does not move statutory obligations. Absent technical documentation, NordBank cannot discharge its own duties — this is a procurement failure to remediate, and Art. 25 addresses information flow along the value chain.

rubric.criterion: Answers the customer under both regimes
rubric.expected: GDPR Arts. 15 and 22 give access plus meaningful information about the logic and the right to contest and obtain human intervention; the AI Act adds an explanation right for Annex III decisions. "Proprietary model" does not defeat either.
rubric.citation: Ch4 §Data Controller Obligations; Ch6 §Transparency and User Instructions

rubric.criterion: Gets the penalty exposure right
rubric.expected: Up to €15M or 3% for high-risk non-compliance — not the €35M/7% band, which is for Art. 5 prohibitions. GDPR exposure runs in parallel at up to 4%.

rubric.criterion: Stops the partner-bank rollout
rubric.expected: Supplying to partner banks makes NordBank a provider to third parties, compounding every unmet obligation. Conformity assessment and documentation must precede rollout.

briefs.title: The framework bake-off
briefs.scenario:
You have joined a 900-person medical devices company as its first AI governance lead. The company builds imaging software with embedded AI, sold in the EU and the US. It already holds ISO 13485 and ISO 27001 certification and has a mature quality management system.

The CTO wants to "adopt the NIST AI RMF because it's free and the Americans use it". The quality director wants ISO/IEC 42001 "because we can certify it and our auditors already know ISO". The general counsel says neither matters because "only the EU AI Act is law". The CEO has asked for a one-page recommendation and is impatient with nuance.

Complicating this: the company's products are Annex I embedded AI under the EU AI Act, not standalone Annex III. Nobody in the room knows what that changes. The board also wants to state something about responsible AI in the annual report and has asked whether the company can say it "complies with the OECD AI Principles".

fields.prompt: Explain the relationship between the AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and the OECD Principles.
Is the general counsel right that only the AI Act matters?
What does being Annex I embedded rather than Annex III change?
Which ISO standards are relevant here, and what does each actually do?
Can the company claim it 'complies with the OECD AI Principles'?
Give the one-page recommendation the CEO asked for.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes binding from voluntary correctly
rubric.expected: The AI Act is binding law with fines. 42001, the AI RMF and the OECD Principles are voluntary; they can evidence compliance but never substitute for it.
rubric.citation: Ch7 §ISO Standards; §NIST AI Risk Management Framework

rubric.criterion: Corrects the general counsel without overstating
rubric.expected: Only the Act is enforceable, but voluntary frameworks shape what regulators and courts treat as reasonable practice, and harmonised standards carry a presumption of conformity.

rubric.criterion: Gets the Annex I consequence right
rubric.expected: Embedded AI in regulated products is assessed through the existing sectoral conformity route (here the medical device regime) rather than standalone AI Act procedures, and it phases in later than Annex III.

rubric.criterion: Names the three core ISO standards accurately
rubric.expected: 22989 terminology and concepts; 42001 certifiable AI management system; 42005 AI system impact assessment guidance. BoK v2.1 names exactly these three.

rubric.criterion: Exploits the existing certifications
rubric.expected: 42001 is designed to integrate with 27001 and 13485 through Annex SL, so the existing management system is the cheapest path — which resolves the CTO/quality director dispute on the merits rather than by preference.

rubric.criterion: Handles the OECD claim honestly
rubric.expected: The OECD Principles are non-certifiable state-directed principles. A company can say it is aligned with them; "complies with" implies a conformity assessment that does not exist, and risks being a deceptive claim.

rubric.criterion: Recognises the NIST AI RMF is not either/or
rubric.expected: The AI RMF and Playbook can structure risk work inside a 42001 management system; the question is not which one, it is which is the system of record.
rubric.citation: Ch7 §NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)

briefs.title: Capstone — Meridian Health, four jurisdictions
briefs.scenario:
Meridian Health operates hospital groups in Ireland, Illinois, South Korea and Brazil. It is deploying a single AI platform across all four: a triage assistant that ranks emergency arrivals by acuity, plus a generative documentation assistant that drafts clinical notes and patient-facing discharge summaries.

The triage model was built in-house in Dublin. The documentation assistant is a third-party general-purpose model above the systemic-risk threshold, accessed via API, fine-tuned on Meridian's own clinical notes, and deployed under the name "Meridian Scribe". Patient-facing summaries are generated and sent automatically unless a clinician intervenes; clinicians intervene in about 4% of cases.

Meridian's Irish entity is the contracting party for the API. Korean patient data stays in Korea. Illinois staff are also screened for internal promotion using a separate AI tool. Brazilian operations were added by acquisition three months ago and have no AI documentation of any kind. The group CISO has proposed "comply with the EU AI Act everywhere — it's the strictest, so we're covered".

It is September 2026. The board wants a governance position before the platform goes live in November.

fields.prompt: Classify each system in each jurisdiction where it operates.
What is Meridian's role for each system, and does it differ by jurisdiction?
Assess the CISO's 'comply with the strictest' proposal.
As of September 2026, which obligations actually bind, and which are still ahead?
What are the three most urgent gaps, and why those three?
State the governance position and the go/no-go recommendation for November.

currency.book: EU AI Act high-risk obligations apply from 2 August 2026, so in September 2026 they would bind.
currency.changed: The Digital Omnibus deferred standalone Annex III to 2 December 2027. Article 50 transparency still applies from 2 August 2026. Korea's AI Basic Act has applied since 22 January 2026 with an enforcement grace period.
currency.exam: BoK v2.1 predates the Omnibus. The exam-correct answer uses the enacted timeline; the practice-correct answer uses the amended one. Answer both and say which is which.

rubric.criterion: Classifies triage as high-risk and separates the documentation assistant
rubric.expected: Emergency triage is Annex III high-risk. The documentation assistant is largely an Art. 50 transparency case for patient-facing output, not automatically high-risk — different systems, different tiers.

rubric.criterion: Identifies Meridian as provider for both
rubric.expected: In-house build makes it provider of the triage model; branding as "Meridian Scribe" plus fine-tuning makes it provider of the documentation assistant despite it being third-party underneath.

rubric.criterion: Dismantles 'comply with the strictest'
rubric.expected: Requirements are not nested. Korea requires a domestic representative and generative-content labelling the AI Act does not; Illinois imposes employment-AI notice duties; Brazil has no comprehensive law but general consumer and data protection law still applies. Strictest-wins produces gaps, not safety.
rubric.citation: Horizon — not in the study guide

rubric.criterion: Gets the September 2026 position right on both tracks
rubric.expected: Enacted track: high-risk obligations live. Amended track: Art. 5 prohibitions and Art. 50 transparency live, Annex III deferred to December 2027. Korea's AI Basic Act live since January 2026. Naming which track is being used is the mark of a correct answer.

rubric.criterion: Flags the 4% intervention rate
rubric.expected: Automatic dispatch of patient-facing clinical summaries with 4% clinician intervention is not meaningful human oversight and is the single highest patient-safety and Art. 22 exposure.

rubric.criterion: Treats the Brazilian acquisition as a due-diligence failure
rubric.expected: Three months post-acquisition with no AI documentation means unknown inventory, unknown third parties and unknown training data — you cannot classify what you have not inventoried.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the Korean localisation and representative duties
rubric.expected: Korea's AI Basic Act requires a domestic representative for qualifying foreign providers and advance notification plus labelling for generative output.
rubric.citation: Horizon — not in the study guide

rubric.criterion: Reaches a defensible go/no-go
rubric.expected: Any recommendation is acceptable if it is grounded: a staged launch that defers automatic patient-facing generation and Brazil pending inventory is the strongest, and 'launch everything in November' is not defensible on these facts.
rubric.citation: Ch6 §Mapping Your Role in the AI Lifecycle
